talks.title: Bye-Bye Query Spaghetti: Write Queries You'll Actually Understand Using Pipelined SQL Syntax
talks.description:
🔊 Recorded at PyData Berlin 2025,

🎓 Transform tangled SQL queries into clear, readable pipelines—discover how Pipelined SQL makes complex data transformations intuitive.

Speakers:
Tobias Lampert

Description:
Tired of deciphering complex SQL queries with nested subqueries and sprawling CTEs? This talk introduces Pipelined SQL, an alternative syntax that lets you write queries as a clear, sequential flow of transformations. Tobias Lampert, an analytics engineer at Lotum, demonstrates how this approach—inspired by data frame APIs like Pandas and Polars—brings top-to-bottom readability to SQL.

Learn how Pipelined SQL eliminates the inside-out data flow of traditional SQL by allowing you to chain operators in any order, apply the same transformation multiple times, and debug queries by running them step-by-step. The talk covers which platforms currently support pipe syntax natively (BigQuery, Databricks, Spark 4.0) and how to use SQL transpilers like SQLGlot to convert pipe syntax to any SQL dialect.

Through practical examples comparing traditional and pipelined syntax side-by-side, you'll see how this approach reduces code complexity, improves maintainability, and makes SQL queries genuinely understandable. Perfect for data analysts, engineers, and scientists who want to write cleaner, more robust SQL code.

talks.title: Causal Inference in Network Structures: Lessons learned From Financial Services
talks.description:
🔊 Recorded at PyData Berlin 2025,

🎓 Learn how to measure causal impact in complex financial networks when randomized experiments aren't possible.

Speakers:
Danial Senejohnny

Description:
Measuring the true impact of wealth planning services on client investment behavior presents unique challenges when working with observational data in network structures. This talk explores practical solutions for applying causal inference techniques when A/B testing isn't feasible. Danial Senejohnny from ABN AMRO shares lessons from real-world financial services, addressing challenges like complex relationship graphs between individuals and companies, staggered treatment timing, and multiple outcome modalities (binary and time-series). The presentation covers propensity score matching to mimic randomization, staggered difference-in-difference methods for treatments administered at different times, and strategies for validating results without ground truth. Key insights include simplifying network structures to units, blocking confounding relationships, and evaluating impact across multiple KPIs. This practical guide demonstrates how to adapt standard causal inference methods to messy real-world scenarios where controlled experiments are impossible.

talks.title: Chris Kucharczyk - How to make public data more accessible with "baked" data and DuckDB
talks.description:
Publicly available data is rarely analysis-ready, hampering researchers, organizations, and the public from easily accessing the information these datasets contain. One way to address this shortcoming is to ""[bake](https://simonwillison.net/2021/Jul/28/baked-data/)"" the data into a structured format and ship it alongside code that can be used for analysis. For analytical work in particular, [DuckDB](https://duckdb.org/) provides a performant way to query the structured data in a variety of contexts.

This talk will explore the benefits and tradeoffs of this architectural pattern using the design of [scipeds](https://docs.scipeds.org/)–an open source Python package for analyzing higher-education data in the US–as a case study.

No DuckDB experience required, beginner Python and programming experience recommended. This talk is aimed at data practitioners, especially those who work with public datasets

talks.description:

Speakers:
Nathaniel Forde

Description:
Nathaniel Forde introduces PyMC Marketing's new consumer choice module, demonstrating how Bayesian discrete choice models can help businesses understand market dynamics and predict consumer behavior. The talk explores the limitations of traditional multinomial logit models, particularly the "independence of irrelevant alternatives" problem that leads to implausible market predictions. Using a heating systems dataset, he demonstrates how these models reveal which product attributes drive consumer utility and enable businesses to safely simulate product interventions and strategy changes. The presentation includes practical examples of causal inference using PyMC Marketing's intuitive API, showing how companies can test pricing strategies and feature additions before implementation.

talks.title: David Brochart - Parallel processing using CRDTs
talks.description:
Beyond embarrassingly parallel processing problems, data must be shared between workers for them to do something useful. This can be done by:
- sharing memory between threads, with the issue of preventing access to shared data to avoid race conditions.
- copying memory to subprocesses, with the challenge of synchronizing data whenever it is mutated.

In Python, using threads is not an option because of the GIL (global interpreter lock), which prevents true parallelism. This might change in the future with the removal of the GIL, but usual problems with multithreading will appear, such as using locks and managing their complexity. Subprocesses don't suffer from the GIL, but usually need to access a database for sharing data, which is often too slow. Algorithms such as HAMT (hash array mapped trie) have been used to efficiently and safely share data stored in immutable data structures, removing the need for locks. In this talk we will show how CRDTs (conflict-free replicated data type) can be used for the same purpose.

talks.title: Democratizing Digital Maps: How Protomaps Changes the Game
talks.description:
🔊 Recorded at PyData Berlin 2025,

🎓 Break free from expensive map APIs: Learn how Protomaps democratizes digital cartography with open-source, self-hosted mapping solutions.

Speakers:
Veit Schiele

Description:
Digital mapping has long been dominated by commercial providers with high costs, usage quotas, and privacy concerns. This talk introduces Protomaps, an innovative open-source project that revolutionizes web map delivery through the PMTiles format—a single-file approach to vector tiles that eliminates complex server infrastructure.

Veit Schiele demonstrates how Protomaps reduces bandwidth usage, improves performance, and makes self-hosted maps accessible without API keys or recurring costs. The presentation covers practical implementations with Leaflet, MapLibre, and OpenLayers, showcasing how developers can integrate Protomaps with just a few lines of code. Real-world use cases include privacy-conscious healthcare applications, offline mapping for crisis areas, and custom municipal infrastructure visualization.

Viewers will learn the complete Protomaps toolstack—from OpenStreetMap data processing to deployment on S3, Caddy, or NGINX—and understand when Protomaps is the right choice versus alternatives like GeoJSON or PostGIS. This technology puts mapping control back in developers' hands while maintaining rich, interactive experiences.

E. Schultz-ActiveTigger: A Collaborative Text Annotation Research Tool for Comp. Social Sciences
talks.description:
The exponential growth of textual data—ranging from social media posts and digital news archives to speech-to-text transcripts—has opened new frontiers for research in the social sciences. Tasks such as stance detection, topic classification, and information extraction have become increasingly common. At the same time, the rapid evolution of Natural Language Processing, especially pretrained language models and generative AI, has largely been led by the computer science community, often leaving a gap in accessibility for social scientists.

To address this, we initiated since 2023 the development of ActiveTigger, a lightweight, open-source Python application (with a web frontend in React) designed to accelerate annotation process and manage large-scale datasets through the integration of fine-tuned models. It aims to support computational social science for a large public both within and outside social sciences. Already used by a dynamic community in social sciences, the stable version is planned for early June 2025.

From a more technical prospect, the API is designed to manage the complete workflow from project creation, embeddings computation, exploration of the text corpus, human annotation with active learning, fine-tuning of pre-trained models (BERT-like), prediction on a larger corpus, and export. It also integrates LLM-as-a-service capabilities for prompt-based annotation and information extraction, offering a flexible approach for hybrid manual/automatic labeling. Accessible both with a web frontend and a Python client, ActiveTigger encourages customization and adaptation to specific research contexts and practices.

In this talk, we will delve into the motivations behind the creation of ActiveTigger, outline its technical architecture, and walk through its core functionalities. Drawing on several ongoing research projects within the Computational Social Science (CSS) group at CREST, we will illustrate concrete use cases where ActiveTigger has accelerated data annotation, enabled scalable workflows, and fostered collaborations. Beyond the technical demonstration, the talk will also open a broader reflection on the challenges and opportunities brought by generative AI in academic research—especially in terms of reliability, transparency, and methodological adaptation for qualitative and quantitative inquiries.

talks.title: Emanuele Fabbiani - Advanced Polars: Lazy Queries and Streaming Mode
talks.description:
Do you find yourself struggling with Pandas' limitations when handling **massive datasets** or **real-time data streams**?

Discover **Polars**, the lightning-fast DataFrame library built in Rust. This talk presents two advanced features of the next-generation dataframe library: **lazy queries** and **streaming mode**.

Lazy evaluation in Polars allows you to build complex data pipelines without the performance bottlenecks of eager execution. By deferring computation, Polars optimises your queries using techniques like **predicate and projection pushdown**, reducing unnecessary computations and memory overhead. This leads to significant performance improvements, particularly with datasets larger than your system’s physical memory.

Polars' **`LazyFrame`s** form the foundation of the library’s streaming mode, enabling **efficient streaming pipelines**, real-time transformations, and seamless integration with various data sinks.

This session will explore use cases and technical implementations of both lazy queries and streaming mode. We’ll also include **live-coding demonstrations** to introduce the tool, showcase best practices, and highlight common pitfalls.

Attendees will walk away with practical knowledge of lazy queries and streaming mode, ready to apply these tools in their daily work as data engineers or data scientists.

talks.title: expectation: A modern take on statistical A/B testing with e-values and martingales
talks.description:
🔊 Recorded at PyCon DE & PyData 2025, April 23, 2025

🎓 Modern statistical hypothesis testing meets game theory in this exploration of e-values and martingales for flexible, valid sequential analysis.

Speakers:
Jako Rostami

Description:
In this presentation, Jako Rostami introduces 'expectation', a Python library implementing modern statistical hypothesis testing using e-values and martingales. The framework offers an alternative approach to traditional A/B testing, based on game-theoretic probability theory. Rostami demonstrates how e-values can be interpreted through a betting/wealth accumulation metaphor, where evidence against a null hypothesis is viewed as accumulated wealth under sequential testing conditions. The framework allows for flexible stopping rules and continuous monitoring without invalidating results, addressing common challenges in practical A/B testing scenarios. Through live code demonstrations, Rostami illustrates the library's application in sequential testing, change point detection, and confidence sequences. The approach maintains statistical validity while offering practitioners more flexibility than traditional p-value methods. A key advantage is the framework's ability to handle sequential testing scenarios while maintaining type-1 error guarantees through Ville's inequality. The library implements these concepts in a modular, object-oriented design with comprehensive documentation and research-based implementations. While positioned as complementary to existing statistical methods rather than a replacement, the framework offers particular value in sequential testing scenarios common in industrial monitoring, finance, and clinical trials.

talks.title: F Gravin - A Journey Through a Geospatial Data Pipeline: From Raw Coordinates to Actionable Insights
talks.description:
Every dataset has a story — and when it comes to geospatial data, it’s a story deeply rooted in space and scale. But working with geospatial information is often a hidden challenge: massive file sizes, strange formats, projections, and pipelines that don't scale easily.

In this talk, we'll follow the life of a real-world geospatial dataset, from its raw collection in the field to its transformation into meaningful insights. Along the way, we’ll uncover the key steps of building a robust, scalable open-source geospatial pipeline.

Drawing on years of experience at Camptocamp, we’ll explore:

- How raw spatial data is ingested and cleaned
- How vector and raster data are efficiently stored and indexed (PostGIS, Cloud Optimized GeoTIFFs, Zarr)
- How modern tools like Dask, GeoServer, and STAC (SpatioTemporal Asset Catalogs) help process and serve geospatial data
- How to design pipelines that handle both ""small data"" (local shapefiles) and ""big data"" (terabytes of satellite imagery)
- Common pitfalls and how to avoid them when moving from prototypes to production

This journey will show how the open-source ecosystem has matured to make geospatial big data accessible — and how spatial thinking can enrich almost any data project, whether you are building dashboards, doing analytics, or setting the stage for machine learning later on.

Starting with rule-based approaches and semantic models, they evolved to a hybrid solution combining OpenAI embeddings for candidate ranking with GPT-4o-mini for final classification. The talk covers critical lessons in prompt engineering, including the evolution from unreliable free-text outputs to structured responses using function calling. Key innovations include using OpenAI's Batch API for 50% cost savings, implementing smart early-stopping mechanisms, and parallelizing category processing. The system now handles 1,500 product updates daily with full automation via Airflow. Results showed significant quality improvements (better precision and recall), enabled 295 new niche categories, and delivered measurable business impact: +1.3% conversion rate, improved quote rate, and reduced bounce rate in A/B testing.

How to use Data Science Superpowers in real life, a Bayesian perspective
talks.description:
🔊 Recorded at PyCon DE & PyData 2025, April 23, 2025

🎓 A data scientist demonstrates how Bayesian inference techniques can enhance personal decision-making, using certification exam preparation as a practical case study.

Speakers:
Tim Lenzen

Description:
In this presentation, Tim Lenzen explores how data science methodologies, particularly Bayesian inference, can be applied to real-life decision-making scenarios. Drawing from his experience as a Senior Data Scientist, Lenzen contrasts workplace data science problems with personal decisions, examining the key differences in data availability, resources, and success metrics. Through a practical example of preparing for a cloud certification exam, he demonstrates how Bayesian modeling using PyMC can transform intuition and limited data into quantifiable decision support. The presentation illustrates the workflow of defining prior distributions, incorporating new data, and deriving actionable insights from posterior distributions. Lenzen emphasizes that while such detailed analysis may not be practical for every decision, the Bayesian framework offers valuable principles for structured decision-making and improved communication about assumptions and evidence. He addresses the challenges of applying these methods to complex life choices, such as career changes or relocations, where metrics are multifaceted and data is scarce. The talk concludes by advocating for the thoughtful application of data science principles to enhance both personal and societal decision-making processes, while acknowledging the importance of managing uncertainty.

talks.title: How We Automate Chaos: Agentic AI and Community Ops at PyCon DE & PyData
talks.description:
🔊 Recorded at PyData Berlin 2025,

🎓 Running a 1500-person conference with volunteers? Learn how PyCon DE & PyData automated chaos with AI agents—and what actually works.

Speakers:
Alexander CS Hendorf

Description:
PyCon DE & PyData volunteers manage a 1500-person conference entirely in their spare time. To survive the chaos of speaker logistics, video processing, ticket management, and marketing, they've built an automation stack powered by AI agents and structured workflows. This talk shares honest, practical lessons from three months of intensive experimentation with agentic AI tools like Claude, Gemini, and various coding assistants. Alexander CS Hendorf reveals what worked (LinkedIn scraping, video cutting with computer vision, API integration), what failed spectacularly (data normalization, multi-step pipelines), and why structure, validation, and narrow scope matter more than hype. With live examples and open-source tools, this case study demonstrates that AI agents are powerful time-savers for boilerplate and well-documented tasks—but they're still 'useful parrots' that need tight guardrails. Perfect for anyone building community infrastructure or exploring practical AI automation.

Kubeflow pipelines meet uv
talks.description:
🔊 Recorded at PyData Berlin 2025,

🎓 Learn how to build maintainable Kubeflow ML pipelines using uv for modern Python dependency management—no more dependency hell!

Speakers:
Fabrizio Damicelli

Description:
Fabrizio Damicelli demonstrates how to combine Kubeflow pipelines with uv, the modern Python dependency management tool, to create more maintainable machine learning workflows. This practical talk addresses a common pain point: managing dependencies across pipeline components while adhering to Python best practices like pyproject.toml and lockfiles. Through live coding, Damicelli shows how to build a simple ML pipeline that runs locally, explaining how Kubeflow orchestrates containerized components on Kubernetes. The key innovation presented is a wrapper solution that dynamically resolves dependencies from uv at pipeline generation time, enabling tools like Dependabot to work while maintaining Kubeflow's flexible API. Viewers learn about component decoration, artifact passing between pipeline steps, and how to structure production-ready ML workflows that avoid dependency conflicts.

Lex Avstreikh - Building Resilient (ML) Pipelines for MLOps
talks.description:
This talk explores the disconnect between MLOps fundamental principles and their practical application in designing, operating and maintaining machine learning pipelines. We’ll break down these principles, examine their influence on pipeline architecture, and conclude with a straightforward, vendor-agnostic mind-map, offering a roadmap to build resilient MLOps systems for any project or technology stack.
Despite the surge in tools and platforms, many teams still struggle with the same underlying issues: brittle data dependencies, poor observability, unclear ownership, and pipelines that silently break once deployed. Architecture alone isn't the answer — systems thinking is.

We'll use concrete examples to walk through common failure modes in ML pipelines, highlight where analogies fall apart, and show how to build systems that tolerate failure, adapt to change, and support iteration without regressions.

Topics covered include:
- Common failure modes in ML pipelines
- Modular design: feature, training, inference
- Built-in observability, versioning, reuse
- Orchestration across batch, real-time, LLMs
- Platform-agnostic patterns that scale

talks.description:
We all love to tell stories with data and we all love to listen to them. Wouldn't it be great if we could also draw actionable insights from these nice stories?

As scikit-learn maintainers, we would love to use PyPI download stats and other proxy metrics (website analytics, github repository statistics, etc ...) to help inform some of our decisions like:
- how do we increase user awareness of best practices (please use Pipeline and cross-validation)?
- how do we advertise our recent improvements (use HistGradientBoosting rather than GradientBoosting, TunedThresholdClassifier, PCA and a few other models can run on GPU) ?
- do users care more about new features from recent releases or consolidation of what already exists?
- how long should we support older versions of Python, numpy or scipy ?

In this talk we will highlight a number of lessons learned while trying to understand the complex reality behind these seemingly simple metrics.

Telling nice stories is not always hard, trying to grasp the reality behind these metrics is often tricky.

The array API standard is unifying the ecosystem of Python array computing, facilitating greater interoperability between code written for different array libraries, including NumPy, CuPy, PyTorch, JAX, and Dask.

But what are all of these ""array-api-"" libraries for? How can you use these libraries to 'future-proof' *your* libraries, and provide support for GPU and distributed arrays to your users? I'll also be sharing progress updates from the past year, to give you a clear picture of where we are now, and what the future holds.

Maintainers of the Future: Code, Culture, and Everything After
talks.description:
🔊 Recorded at PyData Berlin 2025,

🎓 Why the future of tech depends on care, not just code—and how maintenance work is a radical act of resistance.

Speakers:
Jessica Greene

Description:
Jessica Greene challenges tech's "move fast and break things" culture by reframing maintenance as essential, radical work. Drawing from her experience as both a software engineer and PyLadies Berlin organizer, she explores how AI's rapid adoption is creating unsustainable pressures on open-source maintainers while devaluing care work—labor historically gendered and marginalized. Greene examines the hidden costs of AI-generated code flooding repositories, the precarious funding of foundational projects like Python, and how current systems perpetuate inequality. She advocates for pro-social AI development, feminist tech principles, and collective stewardship as alternatives to extractive velocity. The talk connects technical practices like code review and documentation to broader questions of labor, gender equity, and environmental sustainability, arguing that intentional maintenance is how we build resilient, inclusive futures worth inheriting.

Speakers:
Mehdi Ouazza

Description:
This hands-on tutorial explores DuckDB as more than just a DataFrame alternative—it's a powerful in-process analytical database that runs anywhere Python does. Mehdi Ouazza demonstrates how to build data pipelines using SQL without managing servers, reading directly from CSV, Parquet, JSON, APIs, and even PostgreSQL databases. The session covers DuckDB's extension ecosystem, cloud storage integration (S3, HTTP), and seamless interoperability with Pandas and Polars via Apache Arrow. Attendees learn when to choose DuckDB over traditional tools, how to cache intermediate results, and techniques for serving analytics at scale. Real-world examples include analyzing Netflix viewing patterns during COVID, GitHub repository statistics, and Hacker News trends. The tutorial also touches on advanced topics like WebAssembly deployment, MotherDuck cloud integration, and vector search capabilities. Perfect for data engineers, analysts, and scientists working with medium-scale datasets who want lightweight, SQL-based workflows without the overhead of distributed systems.

talks.description:
🔊 Recorded at PyData Berlin 2025,

🎓 How Narwhals enables seamless dataframe interoperability across Pandas, Polars, PyArrow, DuckDB & more—with zero dependencies.

Speakers:
Marco Gorelli

Description:
Narwhals is revolutionizing the Python data science ecosystem by providing a lightweight compatibility layer between dataframe libraries. Marco Gorelli explains how this zero-dependency library enables tool builders to write code once that works seamlessly across Pandas, Polars, PyArrow, DuckDB, PySpark, and more. With 30 million monthly downloads and adoption by major libraries like Altair, Plotly, Bokeh, and Marimo, Narwhals is solving the fragmentation problem that has plagued the dataframe ecosystem. The talk covers the technical architecture, including how Narwhals handles lazy vs eager execution, row ordering, indexing challenges, and SQL compatibility. Gorelli also shares valuable insights on community building, static typing benefits, and the philosophy behind creating a sustainable open-source project. Learn why converting everything to Pandas is a missed opportunity and how meeting users where they are with their preferred dataframe library leads to better performance and fewer bugs.

talks.description:
Nikolai Semiachkin presents a talk on
“LLMs and Prediction Markets: Estimating Probability of Unique Events.”

As data scientists, we are good at predicting regularly occurring events - purchases, clicks, churn. But some events are one of a kind and have a major impact on the world, making them difficult to model with standard data-driven approaches.

In this talk, Nikolai explores how we can estimate the probability of such unique events. He starts with traditional human analytical methods and then shows how large language models (LLMs) and prediction markets can be used to support forecasting, drawing on results from AI forecasting tournaments and recent research.

In this session, Nikolai discusses:
🔹 Why standard predictive models fail for one-time events
🔹 How human reasoning can be structured for forecasting
🔹 How LLMs are being used to automate and support probability estimation

talks.title: Ojas Ankurbhai Ramwala - Explainable AI for Biomedical Image Processing | PyData Seattle 2025
Olivier Grisel - Prediction intervals
talks.description:
Most common machine learning models (linear, tree-based or neural network-based), optimize for the least squares loss when trained for regression tasks. As a result, they output a point estimate of the conditional expected value of the target: `E[y|X]`.

In this presentation, we will explore several ways to train and evaluate probabilistic regression models as a richer alternative to point estimates. Those models predict a richer description of the full distribution of `y|X` and allow us to quantify the predictive uncertainty for individual predictions.

On the model training part, we will introduce the following options:

- ensemble of quantile regressors for a grid of quantile levels (using linear models or gradient boosted trees in scikit-learn, XGBoost and PyTorch),
- how to reduce probabilistic regression to multi-class classification + a cumulative sum of the `predict_proba` output to recover a continuous conditional CDF.
- how to implement this approach as a generic scikit-learn meta-estimator;
- how this approach is used to pretrain foundational tabular models (e.g. TabPFNv2).
- simple Bayesian models (e.g. Bayesian Ridge and Gaussian Processes);
- more specialized approaches as implemented in XGBoostLSS.

We will also discuss how to evaluate probabilistic predictions via:

- the pinball loss of quantile regressors,
- other strictly proper scoring rules such as Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS),
- coverage measures and width of prediction intervals,
- reliability diagrams for different quantile levels.

We will illustrate of those concepts with concrete examples and running code.

Finally, we will illustrate why some applications need such calibrated probabilistic predictions:

- estimating uncertainty in trip times depending on traffic conditions to help a human decision make choose among various travel plan options.
- modeling value at risk for investment decisions,
- assessing the impact of missing variables for an ML model trained to work in degraded mode,
- Bayesian optimization for operational parameters of industrial machines from little/costly observations.

Speakers:
Alina Dallmann

Description:
Alina Dallmann shares practical insights from implementing LiteLLM in a production RAG system for a university chatbot. LiteLLM promises a unified interface across multiple LLM providers, but how does it perform in real-world scenarios?

This talk covers the implementation of LiteLLM's proxy server for a privacy-preserving chatbot serving students and employees. Alina walks through key features including automatic cost tracking, budget management, and load balancing across multiple models. She demonstrates how LiteLLM simplifies provider switching and handles token budgets through PostgreSQL integration.

However, the talk also addresses significant challenges: limitations in custom budgeting requirements, delays in new model support, occasional bugs in new features, and the trade-offs of abstraction layers. Alina provides honest assessments of when LiteLLM excels—multi-provider setups with governance needs—and when alternatives like OpenRouter or TensorZero might be better choices. Essential viewing for developers considering LiteLLM beyond simple prototypes.

talks.title: PyData 2077: a data science future retrospective
talks.description:
🔊 Recorded at PyData Berlin 2025,

🎓 Time travelers from 2077 share a satirical retrospective on data science, AI hype, and imagining better futures beyond dystopia.

Speakers:
Laura Summers, Andy Kitchen

Description:
In this creative and thought-provoking keynote, speakers Laura Summers and Andy Kitchen present a satirical 'time travel' narrative from the year 2077, looking back at the 2020s era of data science and AI. Through humor and speculative fiction, they critique contemporary AI hype, the limitations of correlation-based thinking, and the narrow imagination constraining our field's future. The talk challenges the audience to think beyond dystopian narratives and technological determinism, advocating for causality over correlation, community over tools, and imagination as a core scientific practice. Blending comedy with serious commentary on AI alignment, hyperstition, and the cultural anxieties of our era, the speakers argue that the future isn't predetermined—it's something we actively create through our choices, communities, and willingness to imagine alternatives. The presentation concludes with a call to break free from 'realist mind vices' and recognize that technology serves human flourishing, not the other way around.

talks.title: PyData Stack: Pure Python open source data platforms
talks.description:
🔊 Recorded at PyCon DE & PyData 2025, April 23, 2025

🎓 A practical guide to building production-ready data platforms using pure Python tools, demonstrated through Star Wars franchise analytics.

Speakers:
Eric Thanenthiran

Description:
This presentation examines the implementation of pure Python open source data platforms, focusing on practical architecture and tooling choices for small to medium-scale data operations. Thanenthiran demonstrates the construction of a complete data stack using Star Wars datasets as an example, incorporating five key components: data sources, pipelines, data storage, transformation, and orchestration. The stack utilizes DLT for data pipelines, DuckDB for storage, DBT for transformations, Dagster for orchestration, and Streamlit for visualization. The presentation addresses critical considerations in data platform development, including schema evolution, data quality testing, and lineage tracking. Particular attention is given to the medallion architecture approach, progressing data through raw, staging, domain, and curated layers. The implementation demonstrates handling both API and file-based data sources, transformation logic management, and effective data visualization for non-technical stakeholders. While the demonstrated stack is optimized for batch processing of datasets up to tens of gigabytes, Thanenthiran discusses considerations for scaling and alternatives for larger implementations. The presentation emphasizes practical implementation patterns and real-world considerations in data platform development, providing insights for engineers building initial data infrastructure.

talks.title: Risk Budget Optimization for Causal Mix Models
talks.description:
🔊 Recorded at PyData Berlin 2025,

🎓 Stop chasing highest returns—learn how Bayesian models turn uncertainty into defensible, risk-aware marketing budget decisions.

Speakers:
Carlos Trujillo

Description:
Traditional budget optimization chases the highest predicted returns while ignoring uncertainty, often leading to missed targets and wasted commitments. This talk demonstrates how Bayesian Media Mix Models with PyMC Marketing can transform budget allocation by explicitly accounting for risk. Carlos Trujillo shows how posterior distributions reveal thousands of possible futures, enabling marketers to optimize spending based on risk tolerance rather than point estimates alone. Through practical examples, he illustrates how ignoring uncertainty can lead to allocations with less than 43% probability of hitting targets, while risk-aware optimization using custom utility functions—like mean-times-score or conditional value-at-risk—produces more reliable outcomes. Attendees learn to balance aggressive growth with resilience by encoding risk preferences into optimization objectives, visualizing trade-offs for stakeholders, and making defensible capital allocation decisions grounded in transparent Bayesian reasoning.

talks.description:

This talk presents a case study from Saint-Gobain, in collaboration with Inria, where we applied causal inference methods to production and quality data to reduce raw material usage without compromising product quality.

Sanjiban Sengupta - Advancements in optimizing ML Inference at CERN
talks.description:
At CERN—the European Organization for Nuclear Research—machine learning is applied across a wide range of scenarios, from simulations and event reconstruction to classifying interesting experimental events, all while handling data rates in the order of terabytes per second. As a result, beyond developing complex models, CERN also requires highly optimized mechanisms for model inference.

From the ML4EP team at CERN, we have developed SOFIE (**S**ystem for **O**ptimized **F**ast **I**nference code **E**mit), an open-source tool designed for fast inference on ML models with minimal dependencies and low latency. SOFIE is under active development, driven by feedback not only from high-energy physics researchers but also from the broader scientific community.

With upcoming upgrades to CERN’s experiments expected to increase data generation, we have been investigating optimization methods to make SOFIE even more efficient in terms of time and memory usage, while improving its accessibility and ease of integration with other software stacks.

In this talk, we will introduce SOFIE and present novel optimization strategies developed to accelerate ML inference and reduce resource overhead.

talks.title: Scraping urban mobility: analysis of Berlin carsharing
talks.description:
🔊 Recorded at PyData Berlin 2025,

🎓 Scraping carsharing data reveals hidden urban mobility patterns and opportunities to optimize fleet distribution through user incentives.

Speakers:
Florian König

Description:
Free-floating carsharing systems face a critical challenge: roughly half of vehicles sit idle for three or more hours, contradicting the core purpose of shared mobility. This talk explores how data scraping from Berlin's carsharing operators can reveal hidden patterns in urban mobility and enable smarter fleet management.

Florian König presents findings from analyzing over one million trips across 6,500 vehicles, combining carsharing data with points of interest, traffic conditions, and weather information. Using geospatial analysis techniques like Getis-Ord Gi* and geographically weighted regression, the research demonstrates that contextual factors like POI categories can explain nearly 50% of demand variations on weekdays.

The presentation examines whether low-friction discounts could incentivize users to naturally rebalance vehicle distribution, potentially saving operators significant relocation costs (approximately €10 per manual relocation). While predicting exact destinations proved challenging without user identifiers, the research reveals a theoretical 45% prediction accuracy ceiling if user history were incorporated. The talk offers valuable insights for data scientists interested in urban analytics, transportation modeling, and practical applications of machine learning in mobility systems.

talks.title: See only what you are allowed to see: Fine-Grained Authorization
talks.description:
🔊 Recorded at PyData Berlin 2025,

🎓 Learn to implement fine-grained authorization with OpenFGA for secure, scalable data access control at the resource and user level.

Speakers:
Maria Knorps

Description:
This hands-on tutorial introduces Fine-Grained Authorization (FGA) using OpenFGA, an open-source authorization engine inspired by Google's Zanzibar. Maria Knorps demonstrates how to move beyond traditional role-based access control (RBAC) to implement Relationship-Based Access Control (ReBAC) for data-intensive applications. Participants learn to set up OpenFGA locally, define authorization models using domain-specific language, write relationship tuples, and integrate authorization checks using the Python SDK. The workshop covers practical scenarios like document access management with different permission levels (viewers, editors) across teams and folders. Real-world use cases from highly regulated industries illustrate how FGA enables row-level permissions, handles complex inheritance patterns, and maintains separation of concerns by running as a dedicated authorization service. The tutorial includes live coding exercises, testing strategies, and best practices for synchronizing authorization data with application databases.

Skrub: machine learning for dataframes
talks.description:
Machine-learning algorithms expect a numeric array with one row per observation. Typically, creating this table requires ""wrangling"" with Pandas or Polars (aggregations, selections, joins, ...), and to extract numeric features from structured data types such as datetimes. These transformations must be applied consistently when making predictions for unseen inputs, and choices must be informed by performance measured on a validation dataset, while preventing data leakage. This preprocessing is the most difficult and time-consuming part of many data-science projects.

[Skrub](https://skrub-data.org/) bridges the gap between complex tabular data stored in Pandas or Polars dataframes, and machine-learning algorithms implemented by scikit-learn estimators. It provides scikit-learn transformers to extract features from datetimes, (fuzzy) categories and text, and to perform data-wrangling such as joins and aggregations in a learning pipeline. Its pre-built, flexible learners offer very robust performance on many tabular datasets without manual tweaking. It can create complex pipelines that handle multiple tables, while easily describing and searching rich hyperparameter spaces. As interactivity and visualization are essential for preprocessing, Skrub also provides an interactive report to explore a dataframe, and its pipelines can be built incrementally while inspecting intermediate results.

talks.title: Spot the difference: 🕵️ using foundation models to monitor for change with satellite imagery 🛰️
talks.description:
🔊 Recorded at PyData Berlin 2025,

🎓 Using foundation models and satellite imagery to detect pipeline threats before they become disasters 🛰️

Speakers:
Ferdinand Schenck

Description:
LiveEO's Ferdinand Schenck reveals how geospatial foundation models revolutionize pipeline monitoring through satellite imagery. Operating pipelines buried 1-1.5 meters underground face constant threats from construction, erosion, and unauthorized digging. Traditional inspection methods are costly and inefficient, but very high-resolution satellite imagery (sub-meter ground sampling distance) offers a scalable solution.

The challenge? Distinguishing semantic changes (actual construction threats) from non-semantic changes (shadows, seasonal variations, viewing angles). With limited labeled data—just 1,600 training patches—LiveEO leveraged foundation models pre-trained on vast satellite imagery datasets. Their experiments compared models from ChangeFormer to DINOv2, testing whether geospatial-specific training, ground sampling distance, and model size matter.

Results showed foundation models trained on high-resolution remote sensing data significantly outperformed smaller models and those trained only on natural images. The breakthrough: combining masked autoencoder pre-training with multitask learning on common remote sensing tasks before fine-tuning for change detection. This approach enables accurate monitoring across 60 countries with bi-weekly to bi-monthly revisit rates, protecting critical energy infrastructure at scale.

The EU AI Act: Unveiling Lesser-Known Aspects, Implementation Entities, and Exemptions
talks.description:
🔊 Recorded at PyData Berlin 2025,

🎓 The EU AI Act's hidden exemptions: why high-risk government and law enforcement AI systems escape regulation while commercial uses face scrutiny.

Speakers:
Adrin Jalali

Description:
The EU AI Act is already partly in effect, but many of its most controversial aspects remain under-discussed. Adrin Jalali reveals how the Act exempts military, defense, and national security AI systems from regulation, while law enforcement and border control applications receive special treatment with minimal oversight. Despite categorizing AI systems by risk levels—from banned 'unacceptable risk' systems to heavily regulated 'high-risk' applications—the Act allows companies to self-assess and argue their way out of high-risk classifications. The talk exposes how real-time biometric identification was nearly banned until last-minute negotiations weakened the prohibition, and how notified bodies (private auditing entities) create opportunities for the private sector while raising questions about accountability. Jalali also explores the complex relationship between AI fairness requirements and GDPR, highlighting the ideological challenges in defining and measuring fairness without accessing sensitive personal data.

talks.title: The Importance and Elegance of Polars Expressions
talks.description:
🔊 Recorded at PyData Berlin 2025,

🎓 Discover why Polars expressions are the secret to elegant, efficient data manipulation—they're like Legos for your data pipeline!

Speakers:
Jeroen Janssens

Description:
Jeroen Janssens, co-author of 'Python Polars: The Definitive Guide,' reveals why expressions are the heart of Polars' elegant API. While Polars is famous for speed, expressions make it truly powerful—they're lazy, reusable building blocks that describe data transformations without executing them immediately. This talk covers creating expressions from columns, using them for selection, filtering, sorting, and aggregation, and combining them with operators. Learn how expressions enable parallel execution, query optimization, and cleaner code. Janssens demonstrates idiomatic versus non-idiomatic patterns, explains the tree-like structure of expressions, and shows how they work across namespaces. With real-world examples using fruit data, you'll understand why mastering expressions means you're halfway to mastering Polars. The talk includes audience Q&A covering lazy evaluation, debugging strategies, and comparisons to pandas method chaining and R pipes.

Training Specialized Language Models with Less Data: An End-to-End Practical Guide
talks.description:
🔊 Recorded at PyData Berlin 2025,

🎓 Learn how to train specialized small language models using synthetic data generation—achieving 30-50x size reduction with comparable performance.

Speakers:
Jacek Golebiowski

Description:
This practical talk demonstrates how to train domain-specific Small Language Models (SLMs) using synthetic data generation, eliminating the need for massive labeled datasets. Jacek Golebiowski presents an end-to-end framework using model distillation, where large language models act as 'teachers' to generate training data for smaller 'student' models. Starting with just 10 seed examples and a task description, the approach synthesizes thousands of high-quality training examples through careful validation and deduplication. The result: specialized models that are 30-50x smaller than LLMs while matching or exceeding their performance on focused tasks. Perfect for applications requiring local deployment, low latency, or data privacy—such as PII redaction, classification, and question answering. The talk includes a real-world demonstration of building a PII reduction model and covers practical challenges like data validation, avoiding overfitting, and deployment strategies for production environments.

By the end of this talk, attendees will gain insights into the **practical implications** of model collapse, understanding its impact on content diversity and the long-term viability of AI.

talks.title: What’s Really Going On in Your Model? A Python Guide to Explainable AI
talks.description:
🔊 Recorded at PyData Berlin 2025,

🎓 Learn how to make your ML models transparent and trustworthy using SHAP, LIME, and Captum in this practical Python guide to explainable AI.

Speakers:
Yashasvi Misra

Description:
As machine learning models grow more complex, understanding their predictions becomes critical. This practical talk explores explainable AI (XAI) tools in Python that help data scientists and engineers build transparent, trustworthy models. Yashasvi Misra demonstrates three powerful libraries—SHAP, LIME, and Captum—using the MNIST dataset to show how each tool reveals what's happening inside your models. SHAP uses game theory to show feature contributions globally and locally, LIME provides quick local explanations by perturbing inputs, and Captum offers deep learning insights for PyTorch models. The talk covers real-world applications in healthcare, finance, and operations where explainability isn't optional—it's essential for compliance with regulations like GDPR and the EU AI Act. You'll learn common pitfalls to avoid, how to integrate XAI into your ML lifecycle, and why 72% of organizations now prioritize explainability for wider AI adoption.

talks.title: When Postgres is enough: solving document storage, pub/sub and distributed queues without more tools
talks.description:
🔊 Recorded at PyData Berlin 2025,

🎓 Discover how PostgreSQL can replace MongoDB, Kafka, and Redis—keeping your stack simpler and your team focused on solving real problems.

Speakers:
Eugen Geist

Description:
Software engineer Eugen Geist challenges the impulse to add specialized tools for every new requirement. Instead of reaching for MongoDB for document storage, Kafka for pub/sub, or Redis for queuing, he demonstrates how PostgreSQL's native features can handle these use cases effectively.

The talk covers practical implementations using LISTEN/NOTIFY for pub/sub messaging, SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED for distributed queues, and JSONB for flexible document storage. Geist also introduces vector extensions for AI workloads. Through live Python and SQL demonstrations, he shows how these patterns work in real projects.

The message isn't that PostgreSQL replaces everything forever, but that it can delay the need for specialized infrastructure until truly necessary. For freelancers, startups, and small teams, this approach means faster iteration, fewer operational headaches, and lower costs. By leveraging existing PostgreSQL installations, teams can focus on solving business problems rather than maintaining complex infrastructure stacks.

Dr.  Rebecca Portnoff, Vice President, Data Science, Thorn

Safety by Design for Generative AI: Preventing Child Sexual Abuse

We are at a crossroads with generative artificial intelligence (generative AI). Generative AI is being misused today to further sexual harm against children. 1 in 10 minors report knowing peers that have used generative AI to create explicit images of other kids; 11% of reports of sexual extortion (in which tactics were apparent) to the National Center of Missing and Exploited Children, included threatening children with fake sexual imagery; 50% of Law Enforcement have encountered AI-generated child sexual abuse material used to groom minors; the Internet Watch Foundation observed a 10% increase in sadistic and hardcore AI-generated child sexual abuse material in the material they assessed from 2023 to 2024.

Yet, we find ourselves in a rare moment — a window of opportunity — to still go down the right path with generative AI and ensure children are protected as the technology is built. In a show of powerful collective action, some of the world’s most influential AI leaders have chosen to do just that. In collaboration with Thorn and All Tech Is Human: Amazon, Anthropic, Civitai, Google, Invoke, Meta, Metaphysic, Microsoft, Mistral AI, OpenAI, and Stability AI have publicly committed to Safety by Design principles. This responsible and ethical AI framework guards against the creation and spread of AI-generated child sexual abuse material (AIG-CSAM) and other sexual harms against children.

This presentation will cover the details of this initiative: how strategy has resulted in impact, how this framework for responsible and ethical AI as it relates to child safety has been adopted globally, and how AI governance and responsible AI professionals can pursue this same impact.

talks.title: Ion Stoica, Berkeley: Reliability, an AI challenge
talks.description:
Ion Stoica, Professor & Executive Chairman, University of California at Berkeley, Anyscale

Reliability, an AI challenge

Reliability is a critical obstacle to the successful deployment of AI systems in production. As with conventional software, moving an AI system from prototype to production is far from trivial, requiring robust testing, debugging, and governance. However, unlike conventional systems where components have clear specifications, AI systems—particularly those built on large language models—are black boxes, making failures difficult to detect and diagnose. To address this challenge, we present two systems: LMArena, which evaluates LLMs with real human prompts to measure both accuracy and the impact of style, and MAST, a taxonomy and dataset that reveal why multi-agent systems fail, including poor specifications, misalignment, and weak verification. We argue that achieving reliability requires transforming AI development into a true engineering discipline, grounded in better specifications that are essential for building, debugging, and verifying modular and robust systems.

Developed a NER model to learn the ontology of financial use cases, enabling precise identification of different columns and their        relationships.    ii. Fine-tuned an embedding model to capture semantic relationships between financial entities, improving contextual understanding        of structured data.   c. talks.title: Dr. June Andrews, Lat Long Labs: Optimizing Quality of Life:A Feat of Brute Force and Ignorance
talks.description:
Dr. June Andrews, Founder, Lat Long Labs

Optimizing Quality of Life:A Feat of Brute Force and Ignorance

Lat Long Labs (LLL) presents the first of its kind – a platform for optimizing quality of life as a function of location and family. In this talk, we will dive into the technology enabling this breakthrough—a constraint optimization machine running over a multi-grid feature space that unifies hundreds of maps covering the eight dimensions influencing quality of life: wealth, employment, environment, health, education, recreation, community, and safety. These maps are personalized to family structure, zip code, occupation, and personal interests for all locations in the United States. All together, LLL produces one step closer to data science + machine learning + AI achieving the zenith of what tech can offer us: to optimize the quality of life for every family—every individual—every human heartbeat.

Optimizing quality of life is such a daunting task it can only be embarked upon with brute force and ignorance, until enough building blocks are in place for clever optimization algorithms to take over. LLL’s initial building block was the development of a personalized total tax model encoding thousands of tax laws. It was then augmented with a personalized income estimator and continually refined until achieving the first of its kind – a personalized discretionary income model – calculating generation of wealth as a function of family and location. Mastering personalized financial models is critical to making actionable recommendations. The additional seven dimensions similarly had models developed from basic building blocks to novel representations. Finally, using a technique from mathematical optimization, constrained optimization, good at handling high dimensional spaces with soft penalty functions, a global optimization is possible for quality of life as a function of location and family.

This talk introduces the architecture underpinning the first known model for simulating and optimizing quality of life as a function of location and family. From this model we show a series of case studies linking the theoretical results of the LLL model with real-life challenges and outcomes for families navigating the dynamic landscape of the United States.

talks.description:
Dr. Rodney Brooks, Co-founder & CTO, Robust AI

Getting Robots Deployed at Scale; Robot Demo Videos Are Not Sufficient

It is a golden age for robotics, driven by amazing amounts of compute available onboard, low cost hardware driven by smartphones, electric scooters, and smart appliances, and sixty years of AI advances.  And it is a time where robots are desperately needed as labor is short in manufacturing, warehouse/fulfilment, farming, construction, and many other industries.

Rodney Brooks has been a pioneer in robotics and AI in both academia and in six startups over the last 40+ years. His companies have shipped more robots than any others, and in four major product lines. Now at Robust.AI he and his teammates have developed a new class of mobile robots, driven by AI advances, that radically increase the productivity  of people employed in warehouses and manufacturing, by becoming their most valued tools and making their work much less physically demanding.

AI systems have to satisfy human users. Robots do too, but first they have to satisfy physics, and that is a much less forgiving requirement. talks.title: Dr. Samantha T. Arundel, U.S. Geological Survey: An Intelligent National Map
talks.description:
Dr. Samantha T. Arundel, Senior Science Advisor, National Geospatial Program, U.S. Geological Survey

An Intelligent National Map: Coordinating Structured Analysis and Scientific Validation Across Authoritative Geospatial Data

The U.S. Geological Survey’s National Map provides a consistent, authoritative foundation for elevation, hydrography, transportation, and land cover data across the United States. However, the increasing complexity of spatial problems has outpaced platforms built around static layer access or manual analysis. An Intelligent National Map (INM) is being developed as a modular framework that supports structured queries, coordinated model workflows, and transparent review of analytic results. Rather than serving as a single tool, an INM organizes existing federal datasets into reusable workflows that support spatial reasoning and policy-relevant analysis.
Each workflow is initiated through a user query and proceeds through configured steps for data retrieval, transformation, modeling, and review. All inputs are drawn directly from agency-maintained sources, including the 3D Elevation Program (3DEP), the National Hydrography Dataset (NHD), and land cover datasets such as LCMAP. Results are tied to specific records and returned with complete provenance documentation. Instead of replicating or warehousing data, an INM issues structured queries against live repositories using defined interfaces and schema constraints.
Workflows are carried out by task-specific agents, each aligned to a discrete operation such as model selection, input filtering, or threshold evaluation. Validation is handled by agents configured to compare analytic outputs to published values, ScienceBase records, or ontologically defined spatial relationships. For example, a workflow to delineate flood exposure may combine current stream gauge data with elevation derivatives and surface connectivity metrics to identify risk zones, which are then checked for agreement with hazard maps or published thresholds.
The platform supports use cases in hazard response, infrastructure planning, and environmental monitoring. Examples include wetland persistence mapping based on hydrologic connectivity, optimization of transportation alignments using topographic cost surfaces, and comparison of projected land cover scenarios for zoning evaluation. Results are returned as standardized spatial products along with intermediate diagnostics that document key parameter choices and processing steps.
Every analysis includes a structured explanation layer. Users can view variable contributions, input sources, and references checked by validation agents. Review modules simulate internal steps used in USGS publication workflows, including peer review and policy compliance checks. These are configured using synthetic review personas aligned to the USGS Fundamental Science Practices framework.
Initial development is focused on elevation and hydrography workflows where classification methods and source data are stable. Ongoing work includes refining query interpretation, extending validation loops, and establishing audit mechanisms consistent with governance guidance from the NIST AI Risk Management Framework. Long-term planning includes cross-domain integration and federation across federal organizations.

Jisheng Wang, VP Engineering and Head of AI/ML, Traceable

Securing the New Attack Surface:Navigating the Security Risks and Protection of LLMs

Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently emerged as a cornerstone technology, reshaping every industry and revolutionizing how we interact with digital systems. Much like the advent of network computing and cloud technology before it, the widespread adoption of LLMs heralds a new era of innovation and, with it, a novel attack surface ripe for exploitation. This talk aims to shed light on the inherent security risks associated with LLMs with the real-world examples of LLM-targeted exploitation, and emphasize the importance of proactive threat management in safeguarding the future of LLM-driven applications. Since LLMs will be widely used in future applications, we will first give an overview of the Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) Top 10 Application Risks and Top 10 API Risks which are still applicable to LLMs. Next we will focus on the OWASP Top 10 LLM Specific Risks, and delve into three detailed examples of Prompt Injection, Sensitive Information Disclosure, and Training Data Poisoning. Each example is accompanied by a demonstration of the potential for exploitation, and also the strategies for mitigating these threats and protecting against attacks.

The goal of this talk is to educate the broad AI developer community with the potential risks and vulnerabilities of LLMs and also the knowledge to protect against them, and foster a culture of security that keeps pace with the rapid advancements in AI technology.

talks.description:
Kanika Narang, Research Scientist, Meta

On-Device LLMs: Unleashing the Power of Conversational AI for Mobile and Wearable Devices

Large Language Models (LLMs) have captured the attention of the tech world with their remarkable common-sense reasoning and generalizability. However, their large size and server transfer requirements can make them resource-intensive and slow, which is problematic for use in mobile or wearable devices like smart glasses and smart watches. Moreover, on-device computing could offer a solution to privacy concerns by keeping sensitive data, such as text messages or photos, on the device itself. To tackle these challenges, we’ve developed a more compact language model, ranging from 0.5B to 1.4B parameters. This model is designed to run on-device, providing a competitive performance for conversational grounded tasks, while also managing latency and memory usage effectively.

In this presentation, I’ll delve into our work on creating a versatile, on-device LLM, which is a distilled version of the LLAMA model, specifically tailored for conversational reasoning tasks. I’ll discuss our pretraining framework and our innovative approach to finetuning, which involves using LLM synthesized, task-specific data in a fresh dialogue format. Finally, I’ll share our strategy for scaling our text-based conversational model to a multimodal model, enhancing generative experiences such as composing text replies, document summarization, image captioning, and visual question-answering on wearables or mobile devices.

talks.title: Nir Shavit, Professor of Electrical Engineering Computer Science, MIT: The role of Sparsity in ML
talks.description:
Nir Shavit, Professor of Electrical Engineering Computer Science, MIT

The Role of Sparsity in ML

Our brain executes very sparse computation, allowing for great speed and energy savings. Deep neural networks can also be made to exhibit high levels of sparsity without significant accuracy loss. As their size grows, it is becoming imperative that we use sparsity to improve their efficiency. This is a challenging task because the memory systems and SIMD operations that dominate todays CPUs and GPUs do not lend themselves easily to the irregular data patterns sparsity introduces.

This talk will survey the role of sparsity in neural network computation, and the parallel algorithms and hardware features that nevertheless allow us to make effective use of it.

Subhabrata Mukherjee, Co-Founder and Chief Scientific Officer, Hippocratic AI

Building the first Safety-focused Conversational AI for Healthcare

Healthcare is facing a massive, global staffing crisis. The World Health Organization predicts a 10 million healthcare worker shortage by 2030, but stretched systems and underserved patients are already feeling the effects. Generative AI is the key to closing this staffing gap and ensuring more people can receive a level of care that has never existed before. With generative AI and large language models (LLM) working alongside healthcare workers of all kinds, we are looking to improve access, equity, and outcomes.

Hippocratic AI is building the industry’s first safety-focused LLM for healthcare, specifically focused on non-diagnostic, patient-facing, real-time healthcare conversation. We present Polaris — an agentic trillion-parameter constellation system with collaborative specialization and safety guardrails for human-like conversation. We will talk about the architecture, specialized training and alignment, and the first comprehensive clinician evaluation of an LLM system for healthcare with thousands of U.S. licensed nurses and hundreds of U.S. licensed physicians. We will also share industry use-cases to showcase the best and safest ways to deploy this technology, and explore what AI- and LLM-powered healthcare could look like in the future.

talks.title: Vipul Raheja, Grammarly: Text Revision with Large Language Models -- Challenges and Opportunities
talks.description:
Vipul Raheja, Applied Research Scientist, Grammarly

Text Revision with Large Language Models -- Challenges and Opportunities

Text revision is a complex, iterative process. It is no surprise that human writers are unable to simultaneously comprehend multiple demands and constraints of the task of text revision when producing well-written texts, as they are required to cover the content, follow linguistic norms, set the right tone, follow discourse conventions, etc. This presents a massive challenge and opportunity for intelligent writing assistants, which have undergone an enormous shift in their abilities in the past few years and months via large language models and human-feedback learning. In addition to the quality of editing suggestions, writing assistance has undergone a monumental shift in terms of being prescriptive systems to being human-feedback-driven, collaborative systems. However, writing assistants still lack in terms of their quality, personalization, and overall usability, limiting the value they provide to users.

In this talk, I will present my research, challenges, and insights on building intelligent and interactive writing assistants for effective communication and navigating challenges pertaining to quality, personalization, and usability.

Brain icon for The AI Conference 2023, a groundbreaking two-day event on AGI, LLMs, Infrastructure, Alignment, AI Startups, and Neural Architectures.In our journey of working with our customers to make open source LLMs enterprise ready, we noticed a trend where organizations had a need for both general LLMs and specialized expert LLMs. These expert LLMs are useful in various use cases and scenarios – specialized tasks, context distillation, domain adaptation or incorporating private data. Depending on the complexity of the task, multiple such experts need to come together. However, running them efficiently can be prohibitively expensive. Even with 15 experts at 70b scale, the number of total parameters to hold during inference can easily add up to trillion. We look at how SN40L with its unique hierarchical memory architecture enables faster serving of such a collection of experts, outperforming existing ML hardware providers.

About Urmish Thakker
Urmish leads the NLP Team at SambaNova Systems. The NLP team at SambaNova focuses on understanding how to train and evaluate HHH aligned large language models, adapting LLMs to enterprise use-cases and HW-SW co-design of LLMs to enable efficient training and inference. talks.title: Gradient-Free Structured Pruning With Unlabeled Data, Azade Nova, Research Scientist,Google DeepMind
talks.description:
Gradient-Free Structured Pruning With Unlabeled Data

Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved great success in solving difficult tasks across many domains, but such success comes with a high computation cost, and inference latency. As developers and third parties customize these models, the need to provide efficient inference has increased. Many efforts have attempted to reduce inference cost through model compression techniques such as pruning and distillation. However, these techniques either require labeled data, or are time-consuming as they require the compressed model to be retrained to regain accuracy.

Brain icon for The AI Conference 2023, a groundbreaking two-day event on AGI, LLMs, Infrastructure, Alignment, AI Startups, and Neural Architectures.

In this paper, we propose a gradient-free structured pruning framework that uses only unlabeled data. An evaluation on the GLUE and SQuAD benchmarks using BERTBASE and DistilBERT illustrates the effectiveness of the proposed approach. By only using the weights of the pre-trained model and unlabeled data, in a matter of a few minutes on a single GPU, up to 40% of the original FLOP count can be reduced with less than a 4% accuracy loss across all tasks considered.

About Azade Nova
I am a Senior Research Scientist at Google DeepMind. My research interests lie in the broad area of machine learning, and combinatorial optimization. Currently, my focus is on improving different capabilities of the Large Language models (LLMs). Specifically I am leading the efforts on efficient inference, reasoning, and planning of the LLMs. I have published more than 40 peer-reviewed papers at scientific venues such as Nature, NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR, VLDB, and SIGMOD. Before joining Google, I was a postdoctoral researcher at Microsoft Research in Data Management, Exploration and Mining DMX group.

My research interests are in the broad areas of social network analysis, graph mining, machine learning, data mining, and database. I completed my PhD in Department of Computer Science and Engineering at the University of Texas, Arlington under the supervision of Dr. Gautam Das in Database Exploration Lab (DBXLAB). My PhD research focused on data exploration and analysis over online community networks such as GooglePlus, Twitter, and Amazon and I solved novel problems that have a practical impact and the solutions often involve the design of new techniques or adapting techniques from various fields such as graph theory, algorithms, statistics, etc.

Google AI Residency has given me the opportunity to collaborate with brilliant researcher on challenging machine learning problems. Many important real-world datasets are in the form of graphs or networks: social networks, knowledge graphs, protein-interaction networks, the World Wide Web, etc. (just to name a few). Most of my current research devoted to the generalization of neural network models to such real-world datasets, where the goal is to exploit the graph structure of such datasets in the training process.
