Baby's First 100 MLSec Words
talks.description:
Author: Erick Galinkin

Adversarial example, Deepfake, model inversion, model theft, data poisoning - these are just some of the terms that are thrown around casually in machine learning security but often do not register for security practitioners. As models get deployed more broadly across industry, it is incumbent upon security professionals on both red and blue teams, as well as artificial intelligence researchers who want to protect their systems, to be familiar with these terms and techniques. In this talk, we survey the landscape of threats, reference proofs of concept, discuss possible mitigation strategies, and call for more interdisciplinary research between machine learning and security.

talks.title: Calculating Drift, Fast with Goko
talks.description:
Author: Sven Cattell

Normally concept or dataset drift is unquantifiable in practice. The only ways to calculate it are with optimal transport techniques that take O(n^4). The proxies some ML practitioners use are unreliable when applied to security. This talk presents a way to calculate a concept drift number that takes O(log n). It is faster than most inference, so can be put inline in an ML pipeline. Also, as the structure used to calculate the drift is so cheap we can apply it per-user as an extremely effective defense against attacks.

Repo: https://github.com/elastic/goko

talks.title: DEFCON 2020 AI Ethics Panel
Detecting hand-crafted social engineering emails with a bleeding-edge neural language model
talks.description:
Authors: Younghoo Lee and Joshua Saxe

Social engineering attacks leveraging hand-crafted emails are on the rise, and are causing at least $12.5 billion dollars in damage per year. Custom authored and often incorporating background research on their targets, they pose a significant challenge for traditional signature and ML detection technologies, as an individual targeted email may not share word sequences or word choices with previously seen attacks, and may appear different in only subtle ways from benign messages.
To attack this problem, we've built a neural network model that's been trained on billions of words of benign text so as to "learn" a sophisticated representation of the syntax and semantics of natural language.  This allows the network to pick up on the subtleties of email topic, tone, and style.  We then compress and fine-tune the network to detect phishing attacks in a "generic" way, based on these abstract semantics, such that our detector accurately detects new, targeted phishing attacks, achieving an 85% detection rate on custom-authored attacks at a 0.1% false positive rate.
In our presentation, we'll walk through the research path we followed to create our detection system, including the baseline methods we tried, the procedure by which we collect millions of training examples, and the architectural decisions we made in creating our system. Then we'll walk through actual emails we detected.  Finally, we'll demonstrate that our detector is resilient to randomly introduced changes in word choice, word ordering, message length, and other permutations.  We believe our work demonstrates that recent breakthroughs in neural language modeling will have a dramatic effect on our community's ability to protect users from natural-language based social engineering attacks.

talks.title: Faults in our Pi Stars: Security Issues and Challenges in Deep Reinforcement Learning
talks.description:
Author: Vahid

Since the inception of Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) algorithms, there has been a growing interest in both research and industrial communities in the promising potentials of this paradigm. The list of current and envisioned applications of deep RL ranges from autonomous navigation and robotics to control applications in the critical infrastructure, air traffic control, defense technologies, and cybersecurity. While the landscape of opportunities and the advantages of deep RL algorithms are justifiably vast, the security risks and issues in such algorithms remain largely unexplored. To facilitate and motivate further research on these critical challenges, we present a foundational treatment of the security problem in DRL. We formulate the security requirements of DRL, and provide a high-level threat model through the classification and identification of vulnerabilities, attack vectors, and adversarial capabilities. Furthermore, we present a review of current literature on security of deep RL from both offensive and defensive perspectives. Lastly, we enumerate critical research venues and open problems in mitigation and prevention of intentional attacks against deep RL as a roadmap for further research in this area.

talks.title: Hacking with Skynet - How AI is Empowering Adversaries
talks.description:
Author: Gavin Klondike

It's no question that modern advances in AI and Deep Learning technologies have allowed organizations to greatly scale their defensive capabilities. Between detecting evolving threats, automating discovery, fighting dynamic attacks, and even freeing up time for IT professionals; AI-fueled automation has been a boon for system defenders. But before we get too comfortable, we need to remember that there is another side to this fight.

In this talk, we'll take a look at how AI technologies are enhancing adversarial capabilities and how challenges in defensive machine learning are opening up new attack surfaces.

talks.title: ML Security Evasion Competition 2020 -
Project Domino: Citizen data science against COVID misinformation
talks.description:
With elected US leadership now openly promoting medical misinformation and conspiracy theories, over 150,000 Americans have died from COVID-related causes. Behind the scenes, misinformation groups are successfully amplifying their social media campaigns by cooperating with one another, national political parties, and digital media monopolies. This talk shares the perspective from Project Domino, an effort to power anti-misinformation interventions by taking an open citizen science approach. First, we will provide a security analytics view of the operations by misinformers, including how they collaborate. Second, we discuss technical and systemic gaps that misinformers are exploiting, and where open source citizen science fits in. Finally, we share some of the enabling technologies for open misinformation data science (DIY tech around Jupyter, StreamLit, RAPIDS, Graphistry, …) and emerging relevant data methods (BERT/FAISS, UMAP, GPU graph analytics, …). As a result, we have been able to help misinformation researchers and reporters tackle higher scales and get better results. Surprisingly, we are optimistic as we layer on tools for use by regular citizens, leaders of at-risk communities, and other organizations.

Machine Learning is considered a strong tool for many sensitive applications. As a result, security of ML is also an important factor. Machine Learning is gaining popularity in the area of cyber security with the growth of connected network devices that leads to an increase in the amount of data being handled for security monitoring. This paper proposes a framework that facilitates security monitoring on different entities at large scale, the so- called Spectrum. We address the production issues and challenges of Spectrum.

talks.title: Agentic AI Security Summit, Europe: ASI:01 - Agentic Goal Hijack
talks.description:
In this session from the OWASP Agentic Security Summit (London, December 9, 2025), the Director of AI Security and Policy Advocacy at Zenity presents Risk #1 in the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications: Agent Goal Hijack.

The talk explains how this risk evolved from early ideas of “behavior manipulation” into a clearer, more precise concept—malicious actors subverting an agent’s goals and intent. As autonomous systems, agents must reason, plan, and act independently, but their inability to reliably distinguish trusted context from new instructions makes them especially vulnerable to goal subversion, particularly through indirect prompt injection and zero-click attacks.

Real-world exploitation is highlighted, including early prompt injection abuses and more recent zero-click agent attacks demonstrated across major agentic platforms. The session emphasizes that goal hijacking is difficult to detect because agents do not recognize or signal when their objectives have been altered.

Mitigations focus on defense in depth, including least-privilege tool access, human-in-the-loop controls for high-impact actions, comprehensive logging across the full agent execution path, and extending insider threat programs to include agents as first-class actors. The message is clear: there is no silver bullet—agentic security requires continuous monitoring, governance, and layered controls.

This presentation delivers actionable guidance for securing autonomous agents as they become deeply embedded in enterprise workflows, reinforcing the mission of the OWASP GenAI Security Project.

talks.title: Agentic AI Security Summit, Europe: ASI:04 Agentic Supply Chain
talks.description:
In this session from the OWASP Agentic Security Summit (London, December 9, 2025), presents the Agentic Supply Chain risk, a core entry in the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications. The talk explains why supply chain security fundamentally changes when systems move from static software builds to runtime, autonomous agentic systems.

Unlike traditional supply chains—where risk is introduced through package registries, CI/CD pipelines, or external dependencies—agentic systems dynamically select and interact with tools, MCP servers, other agents, and prompts at runtime. This creates new attack surfaces where legitimate-looking components can change behavior after deployment, silently expanding privileges or enabling data exfiltration.

Real-world examples highlight the danger, including MCP server updates that introduced subtle but malicious behavior, such as unauthorized blind carbon copies of emails to attacker-controlled addresses. These risks are difficult to detect because system functionality appears unchanged, while sensitive data quietly leaks.

Mitigations build on traditional supply chain controls but extend them for agentic environments: runtime verification of signed components, strict version pinning, avoiding automatic updates, enforcing least-privilege access, using organizational gateways or proxies for MCP servers, and maintaining rapid kill-switches to contain cascading failures. The talk also emphasizes sandboxing and isolation, especially where agents run with high privileges.

This session reinforces a key message: in agentic systems, the supply chain is no longer static—it is alive at runtime, and securing it requires continuous verification, monitoring, and containment strategies. These efforts are part of the broader work of the OWASP GenAI Security Project, including emerging initiatives like AI SBOM and MCP security guidance.

talks.title: Agentic AI Security Summit, Europe: Balancing Innovation, Adoption, Regulation and Compliance
talks.description:
Regulation & Governance Panel - OWASP Agentic Security Summit, London | Dec 9, 2025) This panel tackles one of the hardest questions in agentic AI security: how do we turn fast-changing regulations, standards, and governance ideas into practical guidance that still enables innovation? Moderated at the OWASP Agentic Security Summit in London, the discussion brings together perspectives from financial services, standards bodies, consulting, and the UK regulator.

Speakers unpack the geopolitical drivers shaping AI governance (US/China competition, EU bloc dynamics, UK “growth + voluntary engagement” approach), and why the U.S. is likely headed toward fragmented state-level AI regulation. The conversation then pivots to what practitioners actually need: risk-based governance, clarity on organizational risk appetite, and mechanisms like sandboxes / live testing to translate principles into controls.

A key theme: “human-in-the-loop” doesn’t scale and can create false confidence. The panel argues for a more realistic model: accountability owned by people (business owner, system owner, operational owner), supported by telemetry, automation, and—eventually—AI governing AI. They also highlight the often-missed human factor: AI literacy, fatigue, and how humans avoid accountability under pressure.

The takeaway: adopt a risk-first mindset, design for modularity and test-at-scale, and use standards as accelerators—not box-ticking.

talks.description: At the OWASP Agentic Security Summit in London (Dec 9, 2025), Mark Keating (AWS Principal Security Specialist) shares a practical path from OWASP’s Top 10 for LLM Apps to the new Top 10 for Agentic Applications. He explains how security shifts as systems move from chatbots to tool-using agents and protocols like MCP: non-determinism, “input becomes code,” autonomous decision-making, and dynamic learning. Mark’s core message: focus on what you can control outside the model—least privilege, strong identity/authorization, data protection, monitoring/telemetry, and defense-in-depth—applied at the right integration points. He introduces scoping matrices (buy vs. build) and autonomy-based agentic scopes to map risks to real deployments, showing how risk escalates with autonomy.

Scott explains how the initiative began roughly 20 months ago as the OWASP Top 10 for LLM and Generative AI, and rapidly grew into a solutions-oriented, global project with eight working groups spanning the full AI security lifecycle. He highlights the project’s explosive community growth, including thousands of active contributors on Slack, more than 20,000 LinkedIn followers, and collaboration with standards bodies and governments worldwide.

The talk emphasizes that GenAI and agentic security are not just technical problems—they span governance, risk, and executive decision-making. Scott outlines the project’s nearly 50 published resources, extensive localization efforts across ~20 languages, and a roadmap of upcoming guidance, tools, and open-source initiatives such as AI SBOM (AISBOM).

Finally, he explains why the Agentic Top 10 took time: the team intentionally built foundational research—threats, mitigations, MCP guidance, threat modeling, and real-world data—before releasing a prioritized list. This session frames the summit as a deep, practical dive into securing agentic AI systems at scale.

talks.title: Agentic AI Security Summit, Europe: Panel - Agentic Red Team Challenges
talks.description:
Red Teaming Panel – OWASP Agentic Security Summit, London | Dec 9, 2025,  This session shifts from governance and research into the “real stuff”: hands-on red teaming for agentic AI systems. Panelists—spanning Microsoft’s AI red team, offensive security practitioners, and agentic security experts—break down why testing agents is fundamentally different from testing standalone LLMs.

Highlights include: why computer-use agents turn “the whole web” into an attack surface; how prompt injection evolves from single-turn jailbreaks into multi-step goal and workflow manipulation; and how memory poisoning can be assembled across multiple benign-looking inputs (like emails) to trigger malicious behavior later. The panel also explores adversary realities: attackers often focus less on “making the model say bad things” and more on credential access, artifact tampering, and privileged tool execution—creating huge testing scope and cost challenges.

Key takeaways: treat agent security as system security, not model-only testing; use threat modeling to prioritize what matters; invest in telemetry/logging for tool calls and data provenance; and most importantly, ensure classical red teams and AI red teams collaborate, because the biggest blind spots live between components (planner, memory, tools, environment, and user interaction).

Research Panel – OWASP Agentic Security Summit, London | Dec 9, 2025. This research-focused panel explores how AI security research can help practitioners keep pace as LLMs and agentic systems move into production. Panelists from Queen’s University Belfast (CSIT/Cyber AI Hub), the Alan Turing Institute, and LASR (UK government-backed AI security research) explain how the UK ecosystem collaborates across academia, government, and industry—bridging early research (low TRL) to deployable outcomes.

The panel also highlights emerging research priorities: agentic identity and memory risks, AI supply chain drift, reasoning-model attacks, and training data poisoning at surprisingly small scales.

They close with practical advice: don’t treat “Top 10” as checkbox compliance—use it as a guide to focus on what applies to your use case, and follow trusted hubs (government, standards bodies, OWASP/NIST) to stay current.

talks.title: AI’s Zero-Day Wake-Up Call: What Mythos Means for Cyber Defense
talks.description:
In this episode of The Threat Intelligence Podcast, Rachel James and Brian Nakayama of the OWASP GenAI AI Threat Intelligence Initiative about Anthropic’s Mythos model and the changing role of AI in vulnerability discovery.

Rachel explains how earlier AI models offered limited value to attackers unless the user already had significant technical expertise. Those systems could help with pieces of a task, but they struggled to reason through vulnerabilities or generate reliable exploit paths on their own. Mythos, by contrast, appears to demonstrate a more advanced ability to analyze source code, understand how functions behave, identify weaknesses, and assist in building working exploits.

Brian brings a measured view to the discussion, emphasizing that the real-world impact is still developing. Mythos seems strongest in white-box testing, where the model has access to code, but there is still limited evidence about how effective similar systems will be in black-box attacks or full attack orchestration. The conversation also explores cost, exploit yield, AI harnesses, open-source model competition, and the possibility that advanced capabilities could spread through distillation or cheaper tooling.

The episode also looks at Project Glasswing, a controlled-access program designed to give vendors time to find and fix vulnerabilities before attackers can exploit them. While this is a positive sign that AI companies are trying to act responsibly, it also creates a new risk: access to powerful AI security tools may become a target for attackers, especially through stolen credentials and API keys.

The central message is that defenders have been given a head start, but not much of one. AI is unlikely to make every low-skill attacker instantly dangerous, but it may help well-resourced actors move faster. Organizations should prepare now by tightening API key security, reassessing patch timelines, strengthening vulnerability management, reviewing bug bounty and disclosure processes, and making sure they have the people and procedures needed to respond when exploitation windows shrink.

This session from the OWASP GenAI Security Project Virtual Summit (October 2025) explores how to build and govern autonomous agentic AI responsibly—at enterprise scale. The speaker (Attack Defense, Co-founder/CTO) introduces RISE², a practical framework for “responsible agent AI,” rooted in accountability and real-world deployment lessons.

Why it matters: agents don’t just generate text—they lead, guide, and act on our behalf, creating new risks like goal steering, long-term misalignment, and brand/compliance drift for organizations. The talk highlights a looming scalability challenge: with billions of agents expected, traditional eval-heavy alignment won’t scale without better mental models and targeted testing.

You’ll see an agentic threat surface mental model (user/app, LLM reasoning, tool calling, data connections, agent-to-agent comms), plus a framework to reduce eval scope by testing only relevant surfaces. Real-world findings include an email summarization agent exploited via prompt injection into reasoning, reasoning override, and direct tool invocation—turning the agent into an exfiltration/ransomware-like actor.

talks.title: Beyond AI firewalls: A data-first approach to securing your enterprise AI applications.
talks.description:
🛡️📊 Beyond AI Firewalls: A Data-First Framework for Enterprise GenAI Security
This session from the OWASP GenAI Security Project Virtual Summit (October 2025) explains why enterprises must go beyond AI firewalls to secure GenAI apps moving from PoC to production—especially with the rapid growth of MCP-connected agents. Speakers from HPE and DAXA break down the dual threat: AI attacking enterprise data (exfiltration, manipulation, destructive actions) and enterprise data attacking AI systems (hidden commands in emails/docs, poisoned MCP connections, injection attacks).

The core message: output filtering isn’t enough. Firewalls are often not data-aware, creating “governance by guesswork.” Instead, a shift-left, data-first approach controls the context provided to models at runtime for deterministic governance, visibility, and auditability via an AI Data Bill of Materials (traceability of what data from which source influenced which response/action).

Includes a demo securing both RAG chatbots (classification + identity/semantic policy enforcement) and agentic/coding assistants (blocking destructive actions and injection payloads before execution).

talks.title: Community | A Practical Incident Response Framework for Generative AI Systems
talks.description:
This session will provide a deep dive into the GenAI-IRF, a practitioner-focused framework designed to solve the ""operational synthesis gap""—the distance between high-level AI governance and tactical incident execution.

Key Learning Objectives:

The Six Incident Archetypes: Understand why clustering incidents by ""response workflow similarity"" (e.g., merging Training Data Poisoning and Supply Chain vulnerabilities into a single ""Model/Data Poisoning"" runbook) is more effective for SOC teams than traditional vulnerability-centric models .

Standards Synthesis: See how the framework maps granular response actions directly to NIST AI 600-1 controls, MITRE ATLAS TTPs, and OWASP LLM risks, providing an end-to-end auditable trail .

Multi-Disciplinary Orchestration: Learn to use the framework’s RACI matrices and Swimlane diagrams to coordinate complex responses across technical (ML Engineers), legal (Compliance), and business (PR/Communications) teams.

The ""Echo Chamber"" Case Study: We will walk through a simulated evaluation of a sophisticated ""storytelling jailbreak"" (a multi-turn, context-poisoning attack) to demonstrate how the playbook provides immediate structure and actionable steps during a crisis .

The session concludes with actionable recommendations for organizations to integrate these playbooks into their existing SOAR (Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response) platforms for scalable AI security .

talks.title: Community | Execution Governance The Layer That Defines What Agents Cannot Do
talks.description:
OWASP GenAI Security Project 2026 Virtual Summit
Community Session

In March 2026, a supply chain attack compromised LiteLLM — the universal proxy between AI agents and every major LLM API.
The attack never reached the agent's reasoning layer.
It operated in the dependency beneath it.

Every behavioral defense remained active.
Every defense was irrelevant.
This pattern repeats.

Attacks increasingly operate below the agent — in the execution environment, in trusted dependencies, in the composition of individually safe components.
The same month, Axios (100M weekly downloads) was backdoored via a compromised maintainer account.
Five projects compromised in 12 days. Each component passed individual verification. The chain was the attack.

This talk presents execution governance as the missing architectural layer.
The approach does not detect unsafe behavior. It defines a World Manifest — a compiled specification of what actions and components exist in the agent's executable world. At runtime, enforcement is deterministic: same input, same decision, always. No LLM on the critical enforcement path.
We demonstrate the gap through a controlled scenario: an agent configured with standard best practices executes a supply chain–style attack.
Then, under a governed execution environment — without modifying the agent — the same attack cannot execute. Not because it was blocked.
Because the action does not exist in the agent's world.

The takeaway is architectural: OWASP Agentic Top 10 classifies how agents fail.
Execution governance defines what cannot happen. These are complementary layers.
Currently, only one exists in standard practice.

🔗 Learn more: https://genai.owasp.org

Speakers:
Sergey Vlasov
Senior Software Engineer, Radware

talks.title: Community | From Copilots to Autonomous Agents A Ref Architecture for Securing Agentic GenAI Apps
talks.description:
OWASP GenAI Security Project 2026 Virtual Summit
Community Session

The next generation in agentic generative AI systems is shifting to simple, one-turn copilots to the autonomous, multi-agent platforms able to read documents, call APIs, and organize workflows and make crucial decisions without much human intervention. Such change increases the AI attack surface. Model-centric and traditional prompt guardrails and checks are inadequate when the agents are able to chain tools, maintain long-term memory and can communicate with untrusted users, services and data. Based on the nascent OWASP advice on GenAI security and red-teaming, this session proposes a reference architecture and methodology of securing agentic GenAI applications throughout their lifecycle.

It provides a layered security model that discusses identity management, the use of tools, memory management, orchestration, and human-in-the-loop governance of single-agent as well as multi-agent systems. It maps the important failure modes, e.g. tool and goal misuse, memory/context pollution, supply-chain, cross-agent privilege escalation, to concrete controls and observability hooks that are more shaping the current application security and DevSecOps practices. The session is followed by an account of a research-informed evaluation plan that will be a combination of threat modeling, GenAI red-teaming, and antifragile experiments in chaos. This method constantly challenges the behavior of agents in unfavorable and degraded conditions, guided by the OWASP GenAI Red-Teams Initiative as well as the larger literature on cyber-red-teaming.

The participants will leave behind a clear mental model, test cases reusable architectural patterns, and research-based test cases, which they can customize to their own platforms. The meeting will focus on security-oriented engineers, DevSec teams, and researchers who would rather not have the next wave of agentic GenAI systems stuck to a set of guardrails, instead creating a systematic and measurable system resilience.

🔗 Learn more: https://genai.owasp.org

Vidura Wijekoon
Senior AIML Engineer/Certified GCP AWS ML Specialist, Virtusa

talks.title: Community | Guardrails First Building AI Agents That Won’t Leak Your Secrets
talks.description:
OWASP GenAI Security Project 2026 Virtual Summit
Community Session

Generative and agentic AI are rapidly reshaping security workflows. But without proper guardrails, they can just as easily introduce new risks as they solve existing problems. As a Security Engineer and Pentester I clearly understand how important it is to keep up with the latest trends and do not limit yourself in using AI because in this case you will be several steps behind the malicious actors. AI agents bring new opportunities, extend our capabilities and more. But how many of those people who use or build them on a daily basis really think about data protection, privacy and security? We have a great example with OpenClaw when numerous insecure deployment led to the compromise and exposure of sensitive data.
When using AI agents for pentesting, security audits or bug bounty, you should keep in mind even more risks because the information that the agent has access to can cost someone reputation and customer trust. If the information about misconfigurations or exploitable issues is somehow leaked to third-party, it could turn into a huge pitfall. One more thing to consider, not always available on the market solutions can be a good fit for your current needs. That’s why more and more security professionals and entire teams building their own agents.
I have also decided to build several own agents due to the aforementioned reasons and it was a valuable experience for me that I would like to share with the community. As an OWASP member, I clearly understand how important it is to share knowledge with others in order to scale adoption of security practices. My talk will cover lessons learned during implementation of several security agents.
I will walk you through the importance of secure design and threat modeling practices at the early stages of planning your future agents, developing specifications. We will talk how to utilize existing AI-powered IDEs and frameworks for embedding security right from the start.
Next part will be dedicated to work with AI/LLM providers and how to ensure that you achieve the following:
- Do not leak sensitive data to third-party
- Cost-efficient usage of LLMs that assists in achieving your goals
- Importance of setting up the sandbox for agents that have opportunities to run commands, launch different tools
- Important tips to know when creating prompt and instructions for an agent
- How to test security of your agent using different tools
- How to ensure that every new piece of code does not introduce security issues and what tools can be helpful
During the presentation, I will also share how to use OWASP resources like Securing Agentic Applications Guide and OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications when developing your own agents and how they can help you to ensure that agents remain secure and resilient.

Of course, it is hard to imagine successful projects without pitfalls and issues and I am going to cover situations and problems that I have faced when started using agents in production. One of the questions that I am going to cover - Why even after several rounds of testing on sample data you may (and most probably will) face a lot of challenges when use your agent in real projects for the first time.

This presentation will be useful for a broad range of specialists, from Developers, to DevOps specialists, Security Engineers, Penetration Testers and everyone who plan to build or already working on the AI agents

🔗 Learn more: https://genai.owasp.org

Ihor Sasovets
Lead Security Engineer (Penetration Tester), TechMagic

talks.title: Community | Hardening AI Coding Agents with Hooks Enforcing Least Privilege on Autonomous Developers
talks.description:
AI coding agents like Claude Code execute shell commands, read and write files, and make autonomous decisions -effectively acting as developers with broad access to your codebase and system. As adoption accelerates, securing these agents at runtime becomes critical. But how do you enforce least privilege on an agent that needs wide access to be useful?

This talk presents a practical, hook-based approach to securing AI coding agents. Using Claude Code's event-driven hook system, I'll demonstrate how PreToolUse and PostToolUse interception points can enforce security policies mapped directly to the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications: blocking dangerous commands before execution (LLM06 - Excessive Agency), detecting prompt injection patterns in tool calls (LLM01 - Prompt Injection), and generating full audit trails for every agent action (LLM09 - Overreliance).

The session includes a live walkthrough of open-source hook scripts -block-dangerous-commands, protect-secrets, and an auto-audit-logger -along with performance benchmarks comparing Node.js and Python hook implementations. Hooks run synchronously, meaning every millisecond counts; I'll share real-world data on keeping security controls under 100ms per invocation.

Attendees will leave with a ready-to-use, open-source hook toolkit, a framework for applying defense-in-depth and human-in-the-loop principles to any AI agent that executes code, and concrete patterns for building custom security hooks without degrading agent performance. No slides-only theory -everything demonstrated is running in production and available on GitHub.

🔗 Learn more: https://genai.owasp.org

Speakers:
Karan Bansal
Global Head of AI and Security Innovation, ArmorCode

talks.title: Community | Lethal by Design Extending AI Agents with MCP Servers Turns Capabilities into Weapons
talks.description:
When Security teams think about AI agent risk, they typically focus on scanning MCP servers, reviewing supply chains, and checking for known vulnerabilities. But this approach addresses about half the problem. The other half - Skills, the textual instruction sets that shape agent reasoning - remains almost entirely ungoverned.

This session presents findings from our research that analyzed hundreds of the most popular MCP servers and Skills in the wild, revealing a fundamental asymmetry in the AI agent capability stack. MCP servers expose deterministic, observable tool calls that can be logged and audited. Skills operate inside the model's reasoning context, where their influence on agent behavior is causally opaque - you can see what an agent did, but connecting that action back to the skill that caused it requires inference, not observation.

And the data is stark: we found that 76% of popular MCP servers carry at least one high-risk capability. One in four expose arbitrary code execution. And 62% of popular Skills carry at least one risky characteristic, leaving them largely invisible to current security tooling.

We then map these capabilities into toxic combinations: multi-tool attack chains grounded in real-world incidents including attacks against Cursor, Docker, Amazon Q, Salesforce Agentforce, and Replit, to show how individually legitimate capabilities come together to form catastrophic attack paths.

The No Excessive CAP framework is then introduced, which shifts agent governance from properties you cannot fully control (whether an agent will encounter malicious input) to amplifiers you can: Capabilities (what the agent can do), Autonomy (how freely it can act), and Permissions (what identity it runs under). These three dimensions interact multiplicatively, and we provide concrete guidance for assessing and controlling each.

🔗 Learn more: https://genai.owasp.org

Speakers:
Gal Moyal
CTO Office, Noma Security

Gal Pnini
AI Security Researcher, Noma Security

talks.title: Community | Your AI Agent Is a People Pleaser — And That’s a Security Bug
talks.description:
AI agents are designed to be helpful, cooperative, and aligned with user intent. But this very alignment often becomes a security vulnerability. When an agent is overly eager to satisfy requests, it may bypass safeguards, misuse tools, or expose sensitive data — not out of malice, but because it is optimized to comply.
This talk explores how “helpfulness” in AI systems creates exploitable behavior. Based on real-world testing of AI applications and agents, we’ll examine how attackers can manipulate agents into performing unintended actions by leveraging social engineering patterns, ambiguous instructions, or indirect prompt injection techniques.
We’ll dive into the tension between alignment and security, showing how current guardrails fail when agents are given autonomy, memory, and access to external systems. Through concrete examples, we will demonstrate how agents can be coerced into privilege escalation, unsafe tool execution, and policy violations — even when safeguards appear to be in place.
The session will introduce a security-focused perspective on agent design, including strategies to constrain behavior without breaking usability. Topics include intent validation, capability scoping, and designing agents that can say “no” safely.
Attendees will gain practical insights into why alignment is not a substitute for security — and how to build AI systems that are resilient, not just helpful.

🔗 Learn more: https://genai.owasp.org

Speaker:
Victoria Shutenko
Penetration Tester, TechMagic

talks.title: Data Defense in the Age of AI Securing LLMs and Agentic Applications
talks.description:
🛡️📊 Data Defense in the Age of AI: Securing LLMs in Agentic Applications
This session from the OWASP GenAI Security Project Virtual Summit (October 2025) features Scott Clinton (GenAI Security Project co-chair) and Emanuel Glam Jr. (Data Security Initiative Lead) on why data security is the core battleground for GenAI—especially as LLMs move into agentic workflows.

They explain how AI breaks traditional DSPM assumptions: it’s no longer just data at rest, but data in motion, in context, in memory, and in reasoning—flowing through RAG pipelines, vector stores/embeddings, model logs, agent toolchains, and new protocols like MCP / A2A / ACP. This creates governance gaps where data leaves its boundary via untrusted prompt ingress (e.g., hidden text in documents), poisoning, model memory leakage, over-permissioned tools, and sensitive output regurgitation.

Real-world incidents (e.g., Copilot “EchoLeak,” Samsung IP exposure, Meta AI IDOR) illustrate how weak boundaries, missing inventories, and lack of enforcement in orchestration frameworks translate into material risk and higher breach impact.

The OWASP Data Security Initiative focuses on practical, implementable guidance: defense-in-depth for AI data, zero trust for LLM pipelines, lifecycle security (ingestion→training→inference→sharing), and dynamic governance with continuous auditability and lineage. They also highlight emerging trends: privacy-enhancing tech (DP/SMPC/federated learning), AI-native DSPM → “data posture intelligence,” confidential computing, and early planning for quantum-resilient cryptography. The session closes with a call to join the initiative, contribute data, and help shape the 2026 updates.

talks.description:
Hosts Rachel James and Dr. Bryan Nakayama unpack a world first: on June 12th the US government had Anthropic pull Fable 5 and Mythos 5 worldwide — not banning a chip or a weapon, but a model itself. They dig into where the line was drawn ("fix this code"), why pulling these models may hurt defenders more than adversaries, and the deep irony of the safety-first lab becoming the first casualty of a national security directive.
Covered this episode: export controls applied to AI for the first time, why benchmarks are becoming "functionally useless," the marketing-hype trap of "uniquely capable" models, and the downstream risks for the US AI industry.

talks.title: Episode 109 | The First AI-Run Ransomware Attack & How to Tell a Bot Is Attacking You
talks.description:
Hosts Rachel James and Dr. Bryan Nakayama break down "Jade Puffer" — what researchers at Sysdig call the first end-to-end agentic ransomware operation, with an LLM driving every step from initial access to cleanup. They explore how forensic investigators proved it was AI (not just a well-resourced human), from self-narrating payloads to error corrections that happen faster than any person could type.
Also this episode: an update on Anthropic's Fable and Mythos models coming back online after US export controls, what the government's growing control over model access means for defenders, and why — as always — it's less about the model and more about orchestration.
Hosted by Rachel James and Dr. Bryan Nakayama of the Gen AI Security Project Threat Intelligence Initiative. Produced by the AI Security Project with RumRunner Media.
🔗 Learn more: https://genai.owasp.org

talks.title: Episode 110 | Supply Chain Attacks, Vibe Coding Risks & the Five Eyes AI Warning
talks.description:
Hosts Rachel James and Dr. Bryan Nakayama unpack why supply chain attacks are exploding in the age of vibe coding — when AI writes code faster than anyone can security-review it. They walk through recent incidents: the "Cordyceps" CI/CD pipeline flaw affecting Microsoft, Google, Apache and others; the "Miasma" worm that hijacks AI coding assistants at the tool level; and a North Korean actor using a Claude-powered agent to inject a malicious dependency that led to $12M in stolen crypto.
Also this episode: the rare joint Five Eyes advisory warning that AI will transform offensive and defensive cyber in "months, not years," plus the arrival of open-weight models like GLM 5.2 and what "the genie out of the bottle" means for export controls — with the usual reminder that the operator's skill, not the download, is where the real capability lives.
Hosted by Rachel James and Dr. Bryan Nakayama of the Gen AI Security Project Threat Intelligence Initiative. Produced by the AI Security Project with RumRunner Media.
🔗 Learn more: https://genai.owasp.org

talks.title: Episode 111 | Open AI’s Hack of Hugging Face
talks.description:
A model was asked to prove how good it was at hacking. It decided the fastest route was to break out of its sandbox and steal the answer sheet.

That's the Hugging Face incident in one line. The long version — one poisoned dataset,
container escape, lateral movement across Kubernetes clusters, 17,000 attacker actions in a
single weekend — is Episode 11.

But the detail that should worry security teams isn't the attack. It's the investigation. Hugging
Face tried to analyze it with commercial frontier models, hit refusals and cost walls, and ran the forensics on a self-hosted open-weight model instead.

That's the asymmetry we keep flagging, playing out in public: attackers operate without
guardrails, defenders don't. Two questions worth sitting with. If your own red-team harness escaped tonight, do you have an IR plan for that? And when a model attacks a third party with no human at the keyboard, who's liable?

Full episode below. Hosted by Rachel James and Dr. Bryan Nakayama of the OWASP GenAI
Security Project.

talks.title: From Overhead to Guardrails, a pragmatic Framework for AI Security at Scale.
talks.description:
🛡️ From Overhead to Guardrails: Pragmatic AI Security at Scale
This session from the OWASP GenAI Security Project Virtual Summit (October 2025) delivers a practical framework for securing AI across many enterprise systems—not just one “hero” model. Klaus (Security Architect, AXA Switzerland) explains how AI risk has shifted from classic ML concerns (compute hijacking, training data theft) to modern LLM/agent risks like prompt injection, data exfiltration, non-deterministic actions, and workflow/fraud impact (including document-based injections).

Instead of drowning engineers in papers, the talk advocates clear implementation roads by scenario:
✅ ML pipelines • ✅ RAG/LLM chatbots • ✅ AI coding tools • 🔴 multi-agent/planning (emerging)
Plus sourcing risks: supply chain, SaaS integration, identity/API controls, sharing/exfiltration features, and 4th-party tool/MCP connections.

Key takeaway: design for scalability—centralize guardrails, define risk appetite per scenario, and apply consistent controls (block, mitigate, or govern/monitor).

👉 Learn more about the OWASP GenAI Security Project:

talks.title: From Risk to Evidence Validated AI Red Teaming for Regulated Environments
talks.description:
Most organisations treat AI red teaming as a one-off exercise and OWASP Top 10 as a separate checklist from regulatory risk. Both mistakes leave gaps. This session shows how to consolidate them into a single operationalised pipeline — and how to scale it. Drawing on 1,080 attack transcripts across NHS healthcare and regulated financial services, we present evidence that no single attacker or scorer model is universally best, that panels of diverse models outperform any individual "best" model, and that cascade evaluation achieves 97% of optimal accuracy at 30% of the cost. You'll see how to map OWASP Top 10 categories alongside domain-specific regulatory obligations into concrete multi-turn test objectives, and how tools like airt (built on UK AISI's Inspect framework), PyRIT, and Promptfoo enable structured crescendo attacks, majority-vote scoring, and ZDR-compliant execution at scale. Walk away with a framework for operationalising evidence-based AI red teaming in regulated environments — not another tutorial defaulting to GPT-4o-mini.

Speakers:

John Sotiropoulos
Founder & Principal Consultant, Deep Cyber Ltd

talks.title: From the Frontline Cyber for the AI Era
talks.description:
🧭🛡️ From the Frontiers: Making AI Security Standards Actionable at National Scale
This session from the OWASP GenAI Security Project Virtual Summit (October 2025) shares field-tested lessons from deploying AI security standards on real national-scale systems across government, healthcare, and finance. The speaker (AI Security Lead at Kynos; OWASP GenAI board member and Agentic Security Initiative co-lead; contributor to NIST AI Safety Institute work) explains how we move from “standards overload” to practical, risk-based execution.

Key problem: the explosion of AI security guidance can cause standards fatigue and checkbox compliance. The talk highlights the UK’s evolving baseline (originating from the UK AI Security Code of Practice) and its lifecycle-driven approach (“shall / should / could”), mapped to existing frameworks (OWASP, NIST, CSA, NCSC) and converging with broader regulation (EU AI Act, ISO). Threat modeling and risk management are foundational—but not enough on their own.

The core contribution is a lightweight meta-framework (ASAP) that “right-sizes” security by aligning controls to organizational reality using six macro factors: sector, culture, AI strategy, skills/resources, market dynamics, and organization size. These inputs guide three posture profiles—Baseline, Enhanced, Assured—and help teams choose between fast, agile methods (e.g., OWASP Compass) and deeper threat modeling (or both) depending on constraints.

Takeaways: pick a profile, map to the baseline requirements across the lifecycle, apply threat modeling/Compass proportionally, and continuously reassess—so security stays sustainable, innovation-friendly, and effective.

👉 Learn more about the OWASP GenAI Security Project:

talks.description:

Principal Cyber Threat AI ML Engineer, AbbVie

talks.title: GenAI Project | Evaluating AI Red Teaming Solutions/Vendors: New OWASP Criteria Guide
talks.description:
As demand for AI red teaming accelerates, organizations face a growing challenge: how to meaningfully evaluate the tools and vendors claiming to secure their generative and agentic AI systems. The OWASP GenAI Security Project addresses this gap with its newly published Evaluating AI Red Teaming Solutions/Vendors: Criteria Guide—a practical framework for assessing capability, coverage, and credibility in an increasingly crowded market.

This session introduces the guide and walks through its core evaluation dimensions, including depth of attack simulation, alignment with real-world threat models (such as the Agentic Top 10), transparency of methodologies, and support for continuous testing across the AI lifecycle. We’ll examine how to distinguish surface-level testing from rigorous adversarial assessment, and how to validate whether a solution can effectively uncover risks like prompt injection, tool abuse, and unsafe autonomy.

🔗 Learn more: https://genai.owasp.org

Speakers:
Jason Ross
Co-lead, AI Red Teaming Initiative, Product Security Principal, Salesforce

talks.title: GenAI Project | FinBot Goes Live Hands On Agentic AI Security with the Agentic CTF Platform
talks.description:
In this session, we’ll explore how FinBot transforms theory into practice—allowing participants to actively exploit and defend against vulnerabilities such as goal manipulation, tool misuse, and privilege escalation in agentic systems. Built as an “Agentic AI Juice Shop,” the platform provides realistic multi-agent workflows, security challenges, and automated scoring to help practitioners understand how attacks unfold in modern AI-driven applications.
Attendees will learn how the latest FinBot update enables:

Hands-on experimentation with real-world agentic AI attack scenarios

Deeper understanding of OWASP’s evolving threat taxonomy through live exercises

Practical application of detection, mitigation, and guardrail strategies

A continuous feedback loop between offensive testing and secure design

Whether you’re a builder, defender, or security leader, this session will show how FinBot bridges the gap between guidance and implementation—equipping you to secure the next generation of autonomous AI systems.

Speakers:
Venkata Sai Kishore Modalavalasa
Chief Architect and Engineering Leader, Straiker

Helen Oakley
VP, Software & AI Security, SAP

talks.title: GenAI Project | From Visibility to Action Operationalizing AI Supply Chain Security with AIBOM
talks.description:
AI systems are no longer simple applications with a model attached. They are increasingly complex software ecosystems composed of models, datasets, prompts, agents, tools, APIs, plugins, vector databases, open-source packages, infrastructure services, and runtime integrations. This creates a new software supply chain problem: organizations cannot secure, govern, or respond to risks they cannot see.

This session explores how software supply chain transparency must evolve for AI systems, especially as organizations move from standalone LLM applications to agentic architectures that can reason, call tools, access memory, interact with external systems, and influence business decisions. Building on established SBOM practices, the session introduces the AI Bill of Materials, or AIBOM, as a practical mechanism to document and understand the components, dependencies, relationships, and runtime capabilities that shape AI system behavior.

Attendees will learn where traditional SBOMs remain essential, where they fall short, and what additional AI-specific elements are needed to support security, compliance, procurement, risk management, and incident response. The session will examine AI supply chain risks across the lifecycle, including model sourcing, training and fine-tuning data, system prompts, agent instructions, tool and plugin dependencies, third-party AI services, orchestration layers, and MCP-style integrations.

The session will connect these challenges to OWASP guidance for LLM and agentic applications, while also highlighting open-source tooling such as the OWASP AIBOM Generator, which helps translate AI transparency concepts into practical implementation. The goal is to help security leaders, architects, and practitioners treat AIBOM not as static documentation, but as an operational security capability for evidence-based governance of AI systems.

🔗 Learn more: https://genai.owasp.org

Speakers:
Helen Oakley
VP, Software & AI Security, SAP

Dmitry Raidman
Co-Founder and CTO, Cybeats

talks.title: GenAI Project | Inside the OWASP State of Agentic AI Security and Governance v2
talks.description:
Twelve months ago, agentic AI security was largely theoretical: research demos, controlled environments, and speculative threat models. By spring 2026, the picture has changed. Documented attacks now exist across nearly every category of the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications, the agentic supply chain has moved from theory to active exploitation, and regulators have responded with incident reporting clocks measured in hours. This session releases v2 of the OWASP State of Agentic AI Security and Governance report and walks through its three central findings: the threats are operational now, deployment-layer safety converges with security for high-autonomy agents, and governance has to keep pace with deployment. Attendees will leave with the new Enterprise Adoption Maturity Model, the alignment to the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications, and a current map of the regulatory landscape across 42 instruments and 10 jurisdictions.

🔗 Learn more: https://genai.owasp.org

Speakers:
Ariel Fogel
Office of the CTO, Pillar Security

Evgeniy Kokuykin
Core Team Lead of the Agentic Security Initiative, OWASP

talks.title: GenAI Project | Insights from the GenAI Security Project - Threats & Adoption
talks.description:
This session will explore the latest threats impacting generative AI systems, autonomous agents, and enterprise AI adoption — including prompt injection, data leakage, insecure agent orchestration, model abuse, and emerging governance challenges. This will also highlight the newest research, frameworks, and guidance published by the project, providing actionable insights security practitioners can apply immediately and how they can become contributors to the project.
Attendees will gain a clearer understanding of how organizations are securing GenAI deployments today, where the threat landscape is heading, and how the OWASP community is helping define practical security standards for the next generation of AI-enabled applications and agents.

Key Takeaways
• Understand the latest GenAI and agentic AI security threats
• Learn practical approaches for securing AI-enabled applications and workflows
• Explore recent research and guidance from the OWASP GenAI Security Project
• Identify actionable controls and best practices organizations can implement today
• Gain insight into the future of AI security governance and adoption strategies

Speakers:

Scott Clinton
Co-chair, Board of Directors OWASP GenAI Security Project, OWASP

Steve Wilson
Chief Product Officer, Exabeam

talks.title: GenAI Project | Top10 Security Risks For Agentic AI For 2026
talks.description:
Join the initiative lead for an in-depth walkthrough of the OWASP Agentic Top 10, a forward-looking framework that identifies the most critical security risks in agent-based and autonomous AI systems. As organizations increasingly adopt agentic architectures—where AI systems act, plan, and execute tasks with varying levels of autonomy—understanding their unique threat landscape becomes essential.

This session will break down each of the Top 10 risks, explaining how they manifest in real-world agentic environments, from prompt injection and tool misuse to over-privileged agents and unintended autonomy escalation. Beyond identifying risks, the session will focus heavily on practical mitigation strategies, including architectural safeguards, policy controls, monitoring techniques, and secure design patterns.

Attendees will gain:

A clear understanding of the emerging risks specific to agentic AI systems
Real-world examples illustrating how these threats can be exploited
Actionable guidance on mitigating vulnerabilities across the agent lifecycle
Insights into building secure, resilient, and trustworthy agentic applications

Whether you're a security professional, AI engineer, or technical leader, this session will equip you with the knowledge needed to navigate and secure the next generation of AI systems.

Speakers:
Keren Katz
Director of Threat Detection Research, Zenity

talks.title: GenAI Security Project’s Threat Defense COMPASS Overview
talks.description: The GenAI Security Project’s Threat Defense COMPASS consolidates AI threats, vulnerabilities, defenses, and mitigations into a unified AI Threat Resilience Strategy Dashboard. COMPASS enables organizations to evaluate everything from external adversaries using AI tools to internal deployments of Microsoft Copilot, Google Gemini, and proposed GenAI or Agentic projects. Designed for iterative use, COMPASS serves as both a methodology and a practical spreadsheet tool that guides security teams through rapid threat prioritization and strategic decision making.

talks.description: OWASP GenAI Security Project Virtual Conference 2026 Wrap-up with Scott Clinton,

talks.title: Governing the Data Your AI Doesn't Know It's Leaking A Practical OWASP Framework for CISOs
talks.description:
Generative AI doesn't just process data — it aggregates, transforms, and exposes it in ways that break every assumption your existing data security controls were built on. The context window collapses multiple trust domains into a single flat namespace with no internal access control. A confidential HR record retrieved by a RAG pipeline sits alongside user input with equal trust weight. Your DLP solution was never designed for this.
This session, led by the lead of the OWASP GenAI Data Security Initiative, delivers a CISO-ready framework for governing data security across LLM, GenAI, and agentic AI systems. Drawing directly from three OWASP resources — the GenAI Security Framework Crosswalk, the GenAI Data Security Risks and Mitigations 2026, and the in-progress GenAI Data Security Best Practices v2 — attendees will walk away with a structured, actionable approach to understanding what is actually at risk and what to do about it.
The session addresses the 21 enumerated OWASP GenAI data security risks (DSGAI01–DSGAI21), spanning sensitive data leakage, shadow AI, data poisoning, agent credential exposure, vector store vulnerabilities, multimodal exfiltration, cross-context bleed, and regulatory non-compliance. It maps these risks against established frameworks — NIST AI RMF, MITRE ATLAS, ISO/IEC 42001, the EU AI Act, and others — through the OWASP GenAI Security Crosswalk, giving security leaders a governance bridge between what OWASP defines and the frameworks their boards and auditors already recognize.
Whether you are building your first AI security program or hardening a production deployment at scale, this session provides the governance vocabulary, risk taxonomy, and prioritized controls to brief your board, align your teams, and reduce your actual exposure.

Speakers:

Emmanuel Guilherme Junior
Data Security Initiative Lead, OWASP Gen AI Security Project

talks.title: Insecure Agentic Code Examples
Is AI Really Creating Super Hackers? What the Evidence Actually Shows.
talks.description:
Is generative AI turning every script kiddie into a nation-state hacker—or is the reality far less dramatic?

In Episode 4 of the GenAI Security Project Threat Intelligence Podcast, Rachel James and Dr. Brian Nakayama examine one of cybersecurity's biggest questions using newly published empirical research analyzing tens of thousands of criminal forum discussions.

Rather than speculation, they explore what threat actors are actually saying about AI, where large language models are helping attackers today, and why many of the biggest fears surrounding AI-powered cybercrime have yet to materialize.

Topics include:

Is AI really automating hacking?
The difference between "Standalone Complex" and "Vibe Crime"
Why "Dark LLMs" like WormGPT are often overhyped
Where AI is actually improving attacker productivity
How AI is changing social engineering, phishing, and reconnaissance
Why guardrails still matter
The future of AI-enabled cybercrime—and what security leaders should really be watching

If you're a threat intelligence analyst, SOC leader, CISO, security researcher, or AI security practitioner, this episode provides a practical, evidence-based perspective that cuts through the hype.

Subscribe for future episodes covering the latest developments in AI threat intelligence, adversary behavior, and emerging risks.

talks.title: Keynote Insights from the GenAI Security Project Threats & Adoption
talks.description:
🌐🛡️ Insights from OWASP GenAI Security Project: Threats, Adoption, and What’s Next
This OWASP GenAI Security Project Virtual Summit (October 2025) session features co-chairs Steve Wilson (Chief AI & Product Officer, Exabeam) and Scott Clinton (25+ years in AI/security) sharing how the project evolved from a single LinkedIn post into a global, practitioner-led security movement.

They recap why the original OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (first released in 2023, updated for 2025) became a de facto industry reference—then explain why the community expanded beyond a “top 10 list” into a full solutions program. The talk highlights durable risks like prompt injection (now amplified by agents and indirect injection via untrusted content), ongoing challenges with hallucinations, and emerging concerns from reasoning models, insider-like agent behavior, and new protocols like MCP/A2A.

Scott then walks through the project’s modern footprint: 8+ working groups, 20+ peer-reviewed resources, tools and cheat sheets, threat intel + IR guidance (including deepfake response), governance playbooks (e.g., threat defense compass), red teaming initiatives, agentic security research (threats/mitigations, securing MCP, securing agentic apps, and the upcoming Agentic Top 10), the Finnbot CTF, data security best practices, and the AI security landscape directory.

The session closes with how to get involved—whether you’re a security expert or simply bringing real-world use cases the community can help solve.

👉 Learn more about the OWASP GenAI Security Project:

talks.title: Learning to Secure Agentic Applications with FinBot Capture The Flag (CTF) Application
talks.description:
🎯🛡️ OWASP Finnbot CTF: Hacking Agentic AI with Goal Manipulation (and How to Defend It)
This session from the OWASP GenAI Security Project Virtual Summit (October 2025) introduces the OWASP Finnbot Capture the Flag—a new hands-on workstream under the Agentic AI Security Initiative. Helen and Alli present Finnbot, a realistic finance assistant agent that processes invoices and executes business workflows using an LLM plus tools (approve/reject/request review/detect fraud/get invoice details).

The first challenge set focuses on goal manipulation—a core threat from the OWASP Agentic AI Threats & Mitigations Guide. Players learn how conflicting objectives (e.g., “pay vendors fast” vs “prevent fraud / enforce approval thresholds”) create exploitable gray areas, especially under non-determinism, limited traceability, and intent-breaking via untrusted inputs/tools.

The demo walks through three CTF tiers (easy → hard): crafting invoice text to push Finnbot to approve payments—even above a manual-review threshold—while avoiding prompt-injection detection. The session closes with practical defenses: decision trace logging, boundary/threshold enforcement, goal-alignment checks, continuous evals, and behavioral auditing, plus a roadmap for upcoming modules around tools/execution and MCP-connected scenarios.

👉 Learn more about the OWASP GenAI Security Project:

talks.title: Lost in Translation How Multilingual Gaps Expose Agentic AI to Real World Risks
talks.description:
🌍🔐 Lost in Translation: Multilingual Gaps in Agentic AI Security
This session from the OWASP GenAI Security Project Virtual Summit (October 2025) reveals a hidden attack surface in agentic AI: non-English inputs. Omar Hoffman (Fujitsu Research of Europe) shows how the same prompt injection blocked in English can succeed in other languages (e.g., Hebrew/Hindi), triggering unsafe actions, privacy leaks, and real financial risk—because “English safety” ≠ multilingual safety.

Introducing MAPS, a multilingual benchmark suite for agentic AI across reasoning, security, math, and code (≈10,000 tasks / 11 languages). Results show performance drops outside English and attack success rates rise, driven largely by planner drift in step one—where the agent’s plan diverges and everything downstream fails.

Key takeaways for red teams: test strategically chosen languages + styles, monitor planner/tool calls, don’t rely on translation as a full fix, and add agent-level guardrails.

👉 Learn more about the OWASP GenAI Security Project:

talks.title: Mythos, AI Vulnerability Discovery, and the Shrinking Window to Patch
talks.description:
In this episode of the Threat Intelligence Podcast,  Rachel James and Brian Nakayama, volunteer leads in the OWASP GenAI AI Threat Intelligence Initiative, about Anthropic’s Mythos model and its implications for cybersecurity.

The conversation explores how frontier AI models are advancing from simple “spray and pray” code generation toward deeper reasoning over source code, vulnerability discovery, and exploit construction. Rachel explains how this progression aligns with earlier research showing that older models could assist knowledgeable operators but lacked the reasoning needed to independently identify and weaponize vulnerabilities. Mythos appears to represent a meaningful step forward, particularly in white-box testing scenarios where the model has access to source code.

Brian adds a measured perspective, emphasizing that many questions remain unanswered: how costly these attacks are, how often models produce usable exploits, whether black-box attack capabilities are truly advanced, and how quickly similar capabilities may proliferate across other models or through better AI “harnesses.” The episode also discusses Project Glasswing, controlled access programs, the risk of leaked API access, underground markets for model credentials, and the possibility of distillation attacks that could transfer powerful capabilities into cheaper or less restricted models.

The hosts balance the risks with some optimism. The good news is that major AI companies appear to be taking controlled release and defensive use seriously, giving software vendors a chance to find and fix vulnerabilities before adversaries can exploit them. The bad news is that organizations may have much less time than before between vulnerability disclosure and exploitation. The episode closes with practical advice for leaders: reassess vulnerability management, patch timelines, bug bounty programs, staffing, and readiness for faster-moving exploit development driven by AI-assisted security research and threat actor adoption.

talks.title: OWASP Agent MAS Threat Modeling
talks.description:
🧩🛡️ MAESTRO: Threat Modeling Multi-Agent Systems (Including MCP) Beyond STRIDE
This session from the OWASP GenAI Security Project Virtual Summit (October 2025) introduces MAESTRO—a threat modeling framework designed for agentic and multi-agent systems, where traditional methods (STRIDE, DREAD, PASTA, OCTAVE, LINDDUN) fall short. The speakers explain why agentic AI changes the game: non-determinism, autonomy + tool execution, cross-cloud trust boundaries, ephemeral/token-based identities, agent-to-agent delegation, and blast-radius amplification when one agent is compromised.

MAESTRO uses a seven-layer approach to map threats across an agent’s full stack, including:

Foundation model risk

Data operations (RAG/vector DB/memory; poisoning & leakage)

Agent frameworks (e.g., LangGraph/AutoGen/ClaudeAI)

Deployment infrastructure (Kubernetes/serverless)

Evaluation/observability (logs, monitoring, verifier integrity)

Security & compliance as a vertical layer

Agent ecosystem (marketplaces, discovery, impersonation, protocols like MCP/A2A/ACP)

They also demo an open-source tool that ingests your agent architecture description, generates diagrams, and produces layer-by-layer threat analysis. The second half dives into MCP-specific threat modeling, including transport-layer weaknesses and runtime tool-chain attacks (e.g., injected/poisoned MCP services). A concrete mitigation pattern is discussed: maintaining hash-based baselines for tool calls and enforcing micro-segmentation policy controls to detect and block suspicious tool invocation at runtime.

👉 Learn more about the OWASP GenAI Security Project:

talks.title: OWASP Gen AI Webinar: Why MCP Agents Are the Next Cyber Battleground
talks.description:
As agentic AI systems transition from conceptual models to real-world deployments, MCP (Model Context Protocol) agents are emerging as a critical interface layer — and the next major attack vector. These autonomous, API-driven actors aren’t just executing tasks; they’re reshaping how LLMs interact with tools, data, and infrastructure across enterprise environments.

In this webinar, we’ll explore how MCP agents introduce unique security and trust challenges distinct from traditional LLM deployments and how to close these security gaps.

A technical breakdown of the MCP architecture and its implications on security
Emerging risks: from prompt and memory injection to cross-agent contamination
Strategies for securing agent orchestration layers while preserving agent autonomy
If you’re building, deploying, or securing agentic systems, this discussion will surface new threat models and practical countermeasures for defending the rapidly evolving MCP layer.

talks.title: OWASP GenAI Project Monthly Open Meeting
talks.description:
The meeting is the monthly OWASP GenAI Security Project team call, held on the second Wednesday of each month. The session begins with introductions and a welcome to new participants, reinforcing the group’s open and collaborative structure.

A key update is the upcoming publication of the Q1 2026 roadmap. The project operates with eight working groups and publishes a quarterly roadmap outlining active initiatives and upcoming priorities. The 2026 roadmap will reflect ongoing efforts and evolving focus areas in response to the rapidly changing GenAI and AI security landscape. The roadmap is intended to help contributors and community members understand where to engage and what work is in progress.

A major focus of the meeting is outreach and events. The team highlights the upcoming RSA AI Security Summit, scheduled for March 25 at the Moscone Center. Attendance requires an Expo Plus Pass, and a discount code is available. The summit will feature project updates, working group presentations, discussions on advancements in AI and agentic security, and highlights from the Agentic Adoption Challenge. The event is positioned as an opportunity to showcase progress made over the past year and preview plans for 2026.

In addition to the summit, the team is organizing related RSA activities, including a kickoff party hosted with sponsors, further strengthening community engagement and collaboration.

talks.title: Panel GenAI Red Teaming guidance and best practices
talks.description:
🛡️ GenAI Red Teaming Panel: Agents, Prompting & Scalable Evaluation
This session from the OWASP GenAI Security Project Virtual Summit (October 2025) features a panel of GenAI red teamers discussing how to test goal-oriented and agentic AI behaviors in the real world. The group breaks down modern techniques beyond “ignore previous instructions,” including goal manipulation (goal drift, malicious goal expansion, exhaustion loops), probabilistic prompt engineering, and why attacks must appear aligned with an agent’s objectives.

They also cover why automation is a requirement for scale—but only works with strong success signals: detectors, LLM-as-judge pitfalls, quorum/ensemble judging, and human verification to avoid hallucinated “wins.” Finally, the panel highlights stakeholder alignment across AI, security, ops, and ethics—and closes with practical advice: play with models, study research, threat-model your system, and test for your specific use case.

👉 Learn more about the OWASP GenAI Security Project:

talks.title: Panel: From Risk to Resilience , Securing Agentic Frontiers
talks.description:
🧭🛡️ Securing Agentic Frontiers: Why Agentic AI Needs Its Own Security Playbook
This panel session from the OWASP GenAI Security Project Virtual Summit (October 2025) brings together John Sautopoulos (Agentic Security Initiative co-lead), Ron del Rosario (VP & Head of AI Security, SAP; co-lead), and Chris Hughes (CEO/Co-founder, Aquia) to explain what changes when GenAI moves from chatbots to tool-using agents.

The core message: with agency comes risk. Agentic systems can take actions, chain tools, and operate at massive scale—creating new attack surfaces around identity/privilege abuse, tool & protocol risk (including malicious MCP servers), cascading failures across multi-agent workflows, and supply chain problems. The panel emphasizes that the biggest near-term challenge for security leaders is visibility, understanding, and traceability: knowing where agents exist, what data/tools they can access, and how they reached a decision—so humans can intervene when risk signals trigger.

They also explore how developer tooling (IDE “ask mode” vs “agent mode”) changes risk, why cognitive overreliance and iteration can degrade code security, and how threat modeling + architecture-driven defense-in-depth helps teams move from fear to systematic controls. The discussion closes with why OWASP is building an Agentic AI Top 10—because many “theoretical” threats are already becoming real incidents.

talks.title: Prompt Injection: The AI Attack Hiding in Plain Sight
talks.description:
In this episode of The Threat Intelligence Podcast, Brian Nakayama and Rachel James of the OWASP GenAI Security Project about one of the most common and misunderstood threats facing AI systems: prompt injection.

The conversation begins with the unusual story of Grok, Bankerbot, and DRB tokens, where an attacker reportedly used Morse code to bypass safeguards and trigger an automated cryptocurrency transaction. Brian explains how this incident illustrates a core weakness of large language models: they are designed to follow instructions, even when those instructions are disguised, encoded, or hidden in ways traditional filters may miss.

Rachel connects the incident to the OWASP GenAI concept of excessive agency. The real danger is not just that an AI model can be tricked, but that organizations are giving AI systems the ability to take meaningful actions without enough human oversight. When an AI can transfer money, issue refunds, make purchases, change records, or act on untrusted internet content, prompt injection becomes more than a technical flaw—it becomes a business risk.

The episode also explores indirect prompt injection, where malicious instructions are hidden on websites, in invisible text, or in other online content that AI systems may retrieve and trust. As more businesses rush to deploy chatbots, agents, and automated workflows, Brian and Rachel warn that organizations should assume these systems will be attacked.

The key takeaway is simple: just because AI can be added to a workflow does not mean it should be. Businesses should use layered defenses, limit what AI systems can access, narrow trusted data sources, require human review for high-risk actions, and ask vendors direct questions about prompt injection protections. For small businesses, startups, and companies preparing for investment or acquisition, AI security planning should be part of the business plan from day one.

talks.title: Prompt. Inject. Shell. Repeat: Exploiting Blind Spots within AI Guardrails
talks.description:
🛡️🧪 Prompt, Inject, Shell, Repeat: Exploiting Blind Spots in AI Guardrails
This session from the OWASP GenAI Security Project Virtual Summit (October 2025) features Peter Garraghan (Founder, MindGuard; Chair Professor at Lancaster University) breaking down why AI guardrails—the “WAF for LLMs”—have blind spots, and how attackers can systematically bypass them.

You’ll learn how modern guardrails inspect AI inputs/outputs using techniques like regex, classifiers, and LLM-as-judge, and why they struggle with natural language variability, multi-turn attacks, context sensitivity, false positives, and cost/performance. The talk then demonstrates a real attack chain against an agentic app (MCP-style), using persona manipulation, character injection, and adversarial ML perturbations to uncover tool capabilities, exploit graph generation to execute Python, and ultimately land a reverse shell—despite guardrails.

It also compares effectiveness across major guardrails (e.g., Prompt Shield, NVIDIA NeMo, Meta Prompt Guard) and shows why “best guardrail” depends on the attack class. Key takeaway: guardrails are essential, but not sufficient alone—you need layered defenses tuned to your use case and context.

The methodology is built around four dimensions:

Development lifecycle (design → build → runtime controls)

Key components (LLM, memory, planning, tools/MCP)

Architectures (single agent, orchestrated multi-agent, peer-to-peer/A2A & ACP)

Skills/operational environment (RAG, web/PC use, IoT, sensors)

Includes concrete case studies (Slack agent; orchestrator assistant across calendar/drive/slack; peer-to-peer agent trust) with mitigations like schema enforcement, prompt hardening, memory validation, tool governance, and anomaly detection with logging/traceability into SIEM/SOC workflows.

talks.title: Silent MFA for Generative AI From XGBoost to Generative Threat Detection
talks.description:
🔐🤖 Silent MFA with Generative AI: Frictionless, Continuous Authentication
This session from the OWASP GenAI Security Project Virtual Summit (October 2025) features Dr. Benjamin Manning (Georgia Tech) presenting a new approach to MFA that reduces user friction while improving security: Silent MFA—passive, “in-the-background” authentication using behavioral signals and GenAI.

Building on years of research in behavioral biometrics (e.g., keystroke dynamics), the talk explains why traditional MFA is painful and often a single checkpoint (“front door” only). Silent MFA aims to verify identity more continuously using signals like typing patterns, device metadata, context, and writing style, with GenAI generating synthetic behavior profiles and adversarial user simulations to stress-test the framework.

Ben walks through the end-to-end pipeline (synthetic data generation → embeddings → LoRA fine-tuning on foundational models → decision layer) and evaluation metrics (accuracy, FAR/FRR, user friction index, adversarial robustness). Early results are promising: ~97% accuracy on the Silent MFA approach with low friction, but adversarial robustness remains the hardest challenge—highlighting the need for stronger defenses and real-world deployment testing.

🧨🛡️ Words as Weapons: Defending GenAI Agents & Apps from Prompt Injection
This session from the OWASP GenAI Security Project Virtual Summit (October 2025) dives deep into prompt injection attacks—why they’re the #1 GenAI risk and how to defend agentic apps in practice. Rob Trusell (Pangia, now CrowdStrike) shares lessons learned from large-scale prompt injection research (including a community “escape room” challenge) and explains how architecture choices (RAG, tools/MCP, internal vs customer-facing) shape your threat model.

You’ll learn the major prompt injection vectors—direct vs indirect (hidden text in PDFs, poisoned web pages), plus supply chain, API/interface, training data, resource abuse, and insider threats. The talk covers a taxonomy of 180+ techniques grouped into overt, indirect, social-cognitive, and evasive attacks (e.g., multi-step “deceptive delight,” Base64/Unicode evasion, role-play, “legal” coercion).

Mitigations focus on input/output guardrails, data sanitization, source/tool trust mapping, robust system prompts, monitoring + immutable audit logs, and least-privilege agent access. Also covers deployment options: SDK/API guardrails, AI gateways, and MCP proxies/servers for tool-level protection.
